row.name: Mojeque
row.description: Mojeque, or Pampa de las Llamas-Moxeke, is a large archaeological site located in the Casma Province of Ancash Region in northern Peru [1]. The site was first investigated by Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello [1]. His student Toribio Mejia Xesspe discovered large polychrome figures at Mojeque which are a striking feature of the complex [1]. American archaeologists Thomas and Sheila Pozorski studied the site in the 1980s [1]. They placed its construction in the "Initial period", 1800 BC to 900 BC [1]. Moxeke, the main mound, is a stepped pyramid containing at least six platforms [1]. It was about 30 m in height, and almost quadrangular: about 160 by 170 m [1].

row.name: Nine Stones Close
row.description: Nine Stones Close, also known as the Grey Ladies, is a stone circle on Harthill Moor in Derbyshire in the English East Midlands [1]. The purpose of the monument is unknown [1]. Nine Stones Close originally measured 13.7 metres in diameter [1]. In the mid-19th century it had seven stones in its ring, although by the early 21st century that number had declined to four [1]. There are two carved cup marks, a form of rock art, evident on one of the remaining stones [1]. In 1877, William Greenwell and Llewellynn Jewitt excavated at the site, and in the late 1930s the Derbyshire Archaeological Society set two of the orthostats standing again [1].

row.name: Spinsters' Rock
row.description: Spinsters' Rock is a Neolithic dolmen near Drewsteignton in Devon [1]. It is situated on Shilstone Farm west of the village [1]. The dolmen consists of three granite supports rising to between 1.7 and 2.3 metres surmounted by a capstone measuring 4.5 by 3.1 metres [1]. The dolmen collapsed in 1862 but was restored in the same year [1].

row.name: Roman Road from Silchester to Bath
row.description: The Roman road from Silchester to Bath connected Calleva Atrebatum with Aquae Sulis via Spinae, Cunetio and Verlucio [1]. The road was a significant route for east–west travel and military logistics in south-east England during the 1st to 5th centuries [1]. Parts of its route were subsequently followed by earthworks that are presumed to form part of Wansdyke [1]. During the Middle Ages, the road was used by drovers, as well as by merchants and travellers [1]. Margary numbered the road as 53 [1]. Portions of the Roman road are extant, while in other places all apparent vestiges are absent from view [1]. In the early 19th century, Colt-Hoare surveyed and mapped its course from Overton Down (west of Marlborough) to Bath; the rest was only known in isolated sections until a study by Hugh Toller was published in 2013 [1].

row.name: Wichqana
row.description: Wichqana is an archaeological site in Peru [1]. It is located in the Ayacucho Region, Huamanga Province, Ayacucho District [1]. Wichqana lies on a western slope of Uma Urqu north of Ayacucho [1]. Wichqana was active from around 1200-800 BC during the Kishka Pata Period and was a ceremonial center on the central highlands of Peru, on the Ayacucho Valley [1]. The ceremonial center was similar to Cerro Secchin and the centers were built in a U-shape of alternating sized stones [1]. On the site there were semicircle temple structures on artificial mounds which indicates some sort of priestly figure was used [1].

row.name: South Weald Camp
row.description: South Weald Camp was a hillfort based in South Weald, Brentwood, Essex [1]. Roughly circular in plan, the fort covered 2.8 hectares, with a suggested construction date in the late Iron Age, from the 1st century BC to the 1st century AD [1]. The location is associated in this period with the Catuvellauni and the Trinovantes [1]. The camp's defences consisted of a rampart and steep banked slope, with traces of an external ditch [1]. Although for a long time after the Iron Age, the Camp didn't have much use, in the medieval period the fort was used as part of a deer-park and then later used as a WWII training ground [1]. The camp occupies a slight hillslope at approximately 98 metres to 102 metres above sea level [1]. South Weald Camp was listed as a Scheduled Monument in January 1955, on the basis of the general rarity in the UK of slight univallate hillforts [1].

row.name: Wet Withens
row.description: Wet Withens is a Bronze Age henge on Eyam Moor in the Derbyshire Peak District [1]. On gritstone moorland over 300 metres above sea level, the site has clear views of the valley of the River Derwent and Higger Tor [1]. The earthen bank of Wet Withens is over 30m in diameter, making it the largest embanked stone circle in Derbyshire [1]. The 'Chair Stone' is the tallest and most prominent stone with a ledge cut out of its face, appearing as a seat [1]. About 10m north of the henge is a large stone cairn (known as Eyam Moor Barrow) about 27m long and 1m high [1]. Near the middle of the cairn is an unusual cup-marked stone [1]. The cairn's shape indicates that it was likely to have been a prehistoric burial barrow [1]. Wet Withens is also known as Eyam Moor 1 because there are 2 smaller stone circles about 650m to the east [1].

row.name: Bucknowle Roman Villa
row.description: Bucknowle Roman villa is a Roman villa in Dorset [1]. The first villa was constructed on the site during the late 1st century AD [1]. A large aisled hall and a possible bath house were built during the first phase of construction [1]. The aisled hall remained in use until at least the mid 2nd to early 3rd centuries before being rebuilt, and also around this time, a new bath house was constructed alongside six timber-framed buildings which were most likely farm buildings or workshops [1]. During the 4th century, the site contained three large buildings and a bath house [1]. The Bucknowle Roman villa found at Bucknowle Farm is the first substantial villa to be found south of the Purbeck Hills [1]. It was excavated between 1976 and 1991 [1].

row.name: Trou de l'Abîme
row.description: Trou de l’Abîme also known as La caverne de l'Abîme and Couvin Cave is a karst cave located in Wallonia on the right bank of the Eau Noire river in the center of Couvin, Belgium, in Namur province [1]. The site consists of a large two level cave with the entrance on the upper level of the western face of an Eifelian limestone cliff and a large terrace which forms a rock shelter of 50 m width and 5 m depth [1]. Excavations of the cave entrance were first conducted in 1887 and 1902 but the evidence recovered from these is lost [1]. In a series of excavations between 1984 and 1985 Palaeolithic stone artifacts and Pleistocene faunal remains were uncovered [1]. Most of the lithic material is flint which had to be transported to the site from a mine at least 30 km away [1]. Associated with the material was a partial human molar [1]. At the time it was found scientists were unable to determine whether it was Homo sapiens or Neanderthal [1].

row.name: Torberry Hill
row.description: Torberry Hill (also spelled Tarberry Hill and Torbery Hill) is an Iron Age hillfort in the county of West Sussex, in southern England [1]. The hill fort is located within the parish of Harting, within the South Downs National Park [1]. The hill is a chalk spur projecting northwards from the South Downs [1]. The fort was partially excavated in 1948 and from 1956 to 1958 [1]. The fort has been damaged by ploughing in the early post-medieval period, and the rampart survives as a low bank and a largely ploughed-in ditch [1]. The interior of the fort contained a number of infilled storage pits; potsherds recovered from them date them to the Iron Age [1]. Other finds from Torberry Hill include a curry comb, two knives, an iron spearhead and a horn weaving-comb; all these artefacts were placed in Lewes museum [1].

row.name: Danish Camp
row.description: Danish Camp is an Iron Age fortified settlement in Shoeburyness in Essex [1]. The site is in the Gunners Park and Shoebury Ranges nature reserve [1]. This site is classed by Natural England as a 'slight univallate hillfort' [1]. There are two sections remaining of the defensive banks of the settlement [1]. The surviving part of the north-western bank is around 80 metres long, and it has an average height of 2 metres and width of 11 metres [1]. Pottery vessels have been found dating to the Middle Iron Age, around 400 to 200 years BC, together with four round houses and many post holes and pits [1]. The site is called the Danish Camp because it was thought to have been constructed by the Danish Viking leader Hastein, who is reported by the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle to have built a fort at Shoebury in 894; though he might have re-used the existing camp, no evidence has been found of Viking occupation [1].

row.name: Aldgate
row.description: Aldgate was a gate in the former defensive wall around the City of London [1]. Aldgate was "fortified with porticullises and chained" in 1377 due to concerns about potential attacks by the French [1]. Aldgate's defensive functions are known to have been tested twice [1]. A 1585 sketch of Aldgate's north tower reveals an interior room of approximately 16 by 14 foot (4.9 by 4.3 m); its southern sibling probably had similar dimensions [1].

row.name: The Grey Mare and her Colts
row.description: The Grey Mare and her Colts is a megalithic chambered long barrow located near Abbotsbury in Dorset, England [1]. It was built during the Early and Middle Neolithic periods (3400-2400 BC) [1]. The tomb was partially excavated in the early nineteenth century, and was found to contain human bones and several pottery fragments [1]. The monument is part of a group of similar monuments spread across the South Dorset Ridgeway [1]. The burial monument today is a nearly rectangular mound, 24 m long, 1 m high, and tapering in width from 13 m wide at the southeast end of the tomb to 8 m wide at the northwest end [1].

row.name: Knag Burn Gateway
row.description: The Knag Burn Gateway is a gateway which was built into Hadrian's Wall some time after construction of the wall itself, generally acknowledged to be during the fourth century [1]. Knag Burn Gateway is located at the point where Hadrian's Wall crosses the Knag Burn, just to the east of Housesteads [1]. Knag Burn Gateway is one of the few gates through the wall that isn't part of a milecastle or fort [1]. The remains indicate that the structure consisted of a single-lane gateway, with guard-chambers on either side and a gate at each end, thus allowing two-stage controlled passage through the wall [1]. Professor I. A. Richmond suggested that the gateway was constructed to allow trade traffic through the wall some time in or after the fourth century [1]. The gateway was discovered in 1855 and excavated in 1936 and 1988 [1].

row.name: La Chabola de la Hechicera
row.description: The Chabola de la Hechicera is a dolmen in Elvillar, Álava in the Basque Country of Spain [1]. Three large vertical stones support a large horizontal flat stone [1]. Nine large stones form a chamber in a polygonal shape [1]. Jose Barandiaran explored it partially in 1936, finding two stone hammerstones, a polished axe of ophite, fragments of pottery and human remains [1]. The stone lying on top was found broken into three parts, but it was restored and replaced in its assumed original position during the 1974 restoration [1]. The finds are preserved in a museum in nearby Laguardia [1].

row.name: Tres Islas
row.description: Tres Islas is a small pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site 20 kilometres north of Cancuen in Petén Department, northern Guatemala [1]. The main feature of the site is a group of three Maya stelae and an altar [1]. Tres Islas is one of only a few Maya cities that erected dated monuments in the Early Classic period (c. AD 250 - 600) [1]. The early presence of the Emblem glyph that was later associated with the Late Classic Cancuen-Machaquila kingdom indicates that Tres Islas was the Early Classic capital of the kingdom [1]. Preliminary investigations in the area of Tres Islas and Cancuen revealed evidence of inhabitation from the Late Preclassic period (c.400 BC - 250 AD) through to the Late Classic (c.600-900 AD) [1]. The arrangement of the stelae and altar precisely mimics the orientation and relationships of the E-Group astronomical complex at Uaxactun, suggesting that the monument group served a similar purpose [1]. The siting of the stela-altar complex on the edge of an east-facing scarp offers a perfect location for observing the sunrise [1].

row.name: Caballo Muerto
row.description: Caballo Muerto is an archaeological complex located on the northern coast of Peru, in the Moche Valley, in the Laredo District of La Libertad Region [1]. The site is located in the middle sector of the Moche valley on the north shore of the river Moche, about 3 km NE of Laredo, Trujillo and about 20 km from the city of Trujillo [1]. It covers 600 hectares where an estimated two thousand people lived [1]. The archaeological complex of Caballo Muerto features stone and adobe constructions, with mud used as mortar [1]. It consists of a dozen ceremonial buildings on constructed platforms, among them the Huaca de los Reyes [1]. Several of these buildings exhibit a "U-shaped" layout that is common for Cupisnique sites [1]. The walls are decorated with reliefs depicting snakes, cats and other images [1]. The economy of the inhabitants of Caballo Muerto was based on the use of irrigated land reclaimed from the desert [1].

row.name: Rock Carvings at Eidefoss
row.description: The rock carvings at Eidefoss are petroglyphs located near the river Fossen in Nord-Fron Municipality in Innlandet county [1]. The carvings comprise two images of moose, one measuring 31 centimetres and the other 35 centimetres [1]. The rock on which they are carved may have fallen from a west-facing, nearly vertical cliff about 20 metres from the river [1]. When the river is at its normal levels, the rock is well away from the river [1].

row.name: Carrigagulla
row.description: Carrigagulla (Irish: Carraig an Ghiolla) is a megalithic complex 2.9 km north-east of Ballinagree, County Cork, Ireland [1]. Carrigagulla A is an 8-metre-diameter (26 ft) stone circle consisting of 16 standing stones circling a central slab [1]. The Carrigagulla NE stone row consists of five stones, four of which have been moved and are now used as gates [1]. The stone row at Carrigagulla SW is built from three stones, one of which has fallen [1].

row.name: Pant-y-Saer Burial Chamber
row.description: Pant-y-Saer is a Neolithic dolmen near the small town of Benllech in Anglesey, Wales [1]. This burial chamber is partially collapsed with the massive capstone resting on the ground at one end [1]. The remains of fifty-six people who were buried here have been found during excavations [1]. The capstone is large, measuring about 3 m in length and breadth, with a thickness of 0.5 m; it has partially collapsed and rests with one end on the ground and the other end supported by two upright stones, one on the north side and the other on the south [1]. The chamber was originally covered with a cairn or mound, of which traces remain [1]. Excavations show that the cairn was walled at the front and may have been extended for some way at the back [1].

row.name: Hosn Niha Roman Temple
row.description: Hosn Niha is an archaeological site in Lebanon composed of some temples and buildings in the outskirts of the village of Niha [1]. The Hosn Niha site was discovered near the Beqaa Valley and lies at the base of a steep slope [1]. Archaeologists discovered a sanctuary with two temples inside, with one being larger than the other [1]. This sanctuary also contains a church and several cult rooms [1]. A smaller sanctuary and two big quarries were also found further down nearing the village of Niha [1]. Built on a podium facing toward the east, the "Upper Great Temple" of Hosn Niha is composed of a portico with four columns, leading to a cella, and then to an elevated adytum [1].

row.name: Mine Howe
row.description: Mine Howe is an Iron Age subterranean man-made chamber dug 6 meters deep inside a large mound [1]. It is located in the Tankerness area of Orkney, Scotland, about 5 miles (8 km) southeast of Kirkwall, the capital of Orkney [1]. A flight of stone steps descend to a half-landing where they turn back on themselves and further steps descend to a chamber [1]. This chamber is only about 1.3 metres (4 ft 3 in) in diameter but is over four metres high with a corbelled roof [1]. The bottom step into this chamber is 0.9 metres (2 ft 11 in) high and gives it a cistern-like appearance [1]. At the half-landing two subsidiary chambers/passages open out, one above the other [1]. After the 1940s excavations were finished, Mine Howe was covered over and left untouched and nearly forgotten for almost 50 years [1].

row.name: Roman Ruins of Villa Cardillio
row.description: The Roman ruins of Villa Cardillio (Portuguese: Ruinas romanas de Vila Cardílio) is an archaeological site located in central Portugal [1]. The first archaeological interest in the site occurred in 1932; Jalhay and Afonso do Paço began investigating the grounds, cataloguing the built-up environment [1]. The site is located in the rural suburbs of the civil parish of Santa Maria, in the municipality of Torres Novas [1].

row.name: Halangy Down
row.description: Halangy Down is a prehistoric settlement located on the island of St Mary's, in the Isles of Scilly [1]. On the site are the remains of an Iron Age village, two entrance graves, prehistoric field systems, standing stones, post-medieval breastworks, and a Victorian kelp pit [1]. The settlement complex, spanning four narrow terraces, is 50 metres long by 30 metres wide [1]. The remains of the ancient village show evidence of continuous settlement from the prehistoric to the Roman period in Britain [1]. Archaeological excavations conducted in 1935, 1950, and 1964 to 1970, revealed that the first stone structures were built during the Iron Age [1]. The village was made up of a complex of attached stone houses [1]. The excavation findings included Iron Age, Romano-British and Anglo-Saxon pottery; flint and quartz tools; a slate spindle-whorl; several millstones; bronze brooches and iron slag [1].

row.name: Maen Castle
row.description: Maen Castle is an Iron Age promontory fort or 'cliff castle' close to Land's End in Cornwall [1]. Maen Castle is one of only two fortified sites in Cornwall where Early Iron Age pottery has been found [1]. Excavations took place in 1939 and 1948-9 and about 300 sherds were unearthed [1]. The defences comprise a stone rampart, ditch and counterscarp bank built across the neck of the headland, with almost sheer cliffs on two sides and a steep slope on the third [1].

row.name: Castra Martis
row.description: Castra Martis was a Roman fortified garrison in Dacia which became a town and bishopric and remains a Latin Catholic titular see [1]. Castra Martis, named after the Roman god of war Mars, on the modern site of Kula, in Vidin Province in northwestern Bulgaria, served to protect the road through Vrashka Chuka pass in the western Balkan Mountains [1]. It was important enough in the Roman province of Dacia ripensis to become a suffragan of the provincial capital's Metropolitan Archdiocese of Ratiaria, in the sway of the Patriarchate of Constantinople [1]. Its only recorded Suffragan Bishop was Calvus, participant at the Council of Serdica in 343 [1]. In 408, the Huns under Uldin took control of the site during an attack on the Eastern Roman Empire, apparently by treachery [1].

row.name: Dun Grugaig
row.description: Dun Grugaig is a D-shaped dun, or "semi-broch", located about 7 kilometres southeast of the village of Glenelg, Highland [1]. Dun Grugaig stands on the north bank of the Abhainn a’Ghlaine Bhig, in the upper reaches of Gleann Beag [1]. It is in the same valley as the two Glenelg brochs of Dun Telve and Dun Troddan [1]. Dun Grugaig is a D-shaped fortification of a type commonly regarded as a prototype broch or "semi-broch" [1]. The first modern survey was conducted by Henry Dryden in 1871 [1].

row.name: La Milpa
row.description: La Milpa is an archaeological site and an ancient Maya city within the Three River region of Northwest Belize bordering Mexico and Guatemala [1]. La Milpa is located between the sites of Rio Azul and Lamanai [1]. Following Caracol and Lamanai, La Milpa is the third largest site in Belize with the Main Plaza alone covering 18,000 square meters, making it one of the largest in the entire Maya region [1]. At La Milpa during the mid-8th century, there was a steep upward climb in the construction of monumental architecture and the dedication of stelae [1]. The site of La Milpa was occupied from the Pre-classic and Early Classic into the Late and Terminal Classic [1]. La Milpa had intensive agriculture as indicated by extensive terraces [1].

row.name: Pilsdon Pen
row.description: Pilsdon Pen is a 277-metre hill in Dorset in South West England, situated at the north end of the Marshwood Vale, approximately 4.5 miles west of Beaminster [1]. The hill is a lower greensand Cretaceous outcrop situated amongst Jurassic strata of marl and clay [1]. The hill is topped by an Iron Age multivallate Durotrigian hillfort which was excavated in the 1960s by Peter Gelling of the University of Birmingham with his wife Margaret Gelling at the request of the then owner, Michael Pinney [1]. The remains of 14 roundhouses were uncovered near the centre of the hill fort [1].

row.name: Caves of Poço Velho
row.description: The Caves of Poço Velho are located in the centre of Cascais in the Lisbon district of Portugal [1]. The caves were first explored in 1879 by the geologist, Carlos Ribeiro [1]. However, subsequent work has found that the main occupation of the caves took place in the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods (4th and 3rd millennia BC) [1]. Evidence points to their use as a necropolis, with around 115 burials having been identified [1]. In 1942, Afonso do Paço carried out the second major exploration of the caves and between 1945 and 1947, the archaeologist, Abreu Nunes, carried out new excavations that discovered different funerary remains, including: polished and chipped stone artefacts; limestone votive offerings, such as cylindrical idols; decorated schist slabs, and ceramics [1].

row.name: Swinside
row.description: Swinside, which is also known as Sunkenkirk and Swineshead, is a stone circle lying beside Swinside Fell, part of Black Combe in southern Cumbria [1]. The stone circle at Swinside is located in the south-west corner of the Lake District in the ancient district of Millom, 5 miles north of the town of Millom [1]. The stones used in the construction of Swinside were porphyritic slate collected from the adjacent fells, and are of the type that was known locally as "grey cobbles" by the 20th century [1]. Swinside's builders included a well defined entrance, 2.1 m wide, at the south-eastern side, which is defined by the placing of two large portal stones outside the circumference of the circle [1]. Such portal openings can also be found at Long Meg and Her Daughters, 64 km to the northeast in the Eden Valley [1]. In 1901, the Cumberland & Westmorland Antiquarian & Archaeological Society sponsored the first archaeological excavation at Swinside [1]. The excavators reported finding a lump of charcoal and a piece of decayed bone as well as some modern coins in the turf layer [1].

row.name: Arch of Augustus
row.description: The Arch of Augustus is a monument in the city of Aosta, northern Italy [1]. It was erected in 25 BC on the occasion of the Roman victory over the Salassi and was the work of Aulus Terentius Varro Murena [1]. It is located at the end of the decumanus maximus [1]. Constructed from conglomerate, the arch has a single vault, with a height to the keystone of 11.4 metres [1]. Its span is a barrel vault, constituting an extension in width of a round arch [1]. In the monument, various styles can be recognised: The ten engaged columns which decorate its facade and its sides culminate in Corinthian capitals, while the entablature, adorned with metopes and triglyphs, is of the Doric order [1]. During the 12th century, the arch contained the home of a local noble family and in 1318 a small fortification was built inside it, designed for a corps of crossbowmen [1]. In 1716, because of the numerous leaks that were compromising the integrity of the monument, the attic that previously crowned the arch was replaced with a slate roof [1].

row.name: Castlenalacht Stone Row
row.description: Castlenalacht Stone Row is an alignment of four tall and free-standing stones located on a hilltop in the townland of Castlenalacht, Innishannon parish, 6 km north of Bandon, County Cork [1]. It dates from the Bronze Age (c. 3000–4000 years ago) and is the largest of the over 80 stone rows in south-west Ireland [1]. The four Castlenalacht stones are arranged in ascending order of height across a distance of 13.4 m [1]. The site is placed on one of the area's highest hilltops; according to the archaeologist Clive Ruggles, the builders tended to favour locations where the axis, from largest to smallest stone, leads to a relatively distant horizon [1]. The precise functions of these constructions are unknown; most archaeologists assume a ceremonial or ritualistic purpose [1].

row.name: Maes Knoll
row.description: Maes Knoll is an Iron Age hill fort in Somerset, England, located at the eastern end of the Dundry Down ridge, south of the city of Bristol and north of the village of Norton Malreward near the eastern side of Dundry Hill [1]. It is a Scheduled Ancient Monument [1]. The underlying rocks are Inferior Oolite of the Jurassic period [1]. The name Maes Knoll is derived from the Brythonic word *maɣes meaning flat top, derived from Proto-Celtic *magos meaning plain, field, and Old English knoll or knowle meaning hill [1].

row.name: Pikimachay
row.description: Piki Mach'ay (Quechua piki flea, mach'ay cave, "flea cave", also spelled Pikimachay, Piquimachay, where machay means "drunkenness", "to get drunk" or "a spindle packed with thread") is an archaeological site in the Ayacucho Valley of Peru [1]. Richard S. MacNeish was the first archaeologist to explore Piki Mach'ay [1]. The cave is part of the Ayacucho complex, a culture defined by several cave sites including Jaya Mach'ay [1]. Piki Mach'ay yielded some of the oldest plant remains in Peru, including an 11,000-year-old bottle gourd [1]. Strata from later periods at the site revealed fishtail point arrows, manos, and metates [1].

row.name: Kompoloi
row.description: In the plain of Leivithra in 1997 began the excavation work on the ancient winery Kompoloi [1]. They lasted (intermittently) until October 2000 [1]. The building was erected in the middle of the 4th century BC and used until the beginning of the 3rd century BC; then it was destroyed by a fire and abandoned by its inhabitants [1]. It has a floor area of around 1350 m2 and was built on an existing vineyard [1]. The excavated building had 17 rooms [1]. Next to the southern entrance was a well and an oven [1]. Clay pots, pithoi, in which the wine was stored were buried in the ground [1]. In total, 32 of these vessels were found [1].

row.name: Ladle Hill
row.description: Ladle Hill is perhaps the best known of all of the unfinished hillforts in Britain [1]. It was first correctly identified as an unfinished hillfort and described in detail by the archaeologist Stuart Piggott in 1931 [1]. At Ladle Hill it has long been suspected that the area demarcated by the unfinished earthworks never actually contained a settlement, although there is a possibility that the hillfort was to be constructed over an earlier unenclosed settlement [1]. Apart from the dumps of material associated with the abandoned construction works, the interior has very few other earthworks of intelligible character [1].

row.name: Piddington Roman Villa
row.description: Piddington Roman Villa is the remains of a large Roman villa at Piddington, Northamptonshire, about 6 miles south-east of Northampton [1]. The villa is on the site of an earlier late Iron Age settlement [1]. A late Iron Age settlement originated around the middle of the 1st century BC where people lived in round houses inside an enclosure with an outer ditch for protection [1]. The site was occupied from about 50 BC, with circular buildings followed by a proto-villa of ca.70 AD and then a sequence of rectangular stone-built structures, culminating in a simple cottage type villa [1]. From the 2nd century this became an increasingly large winged-corridor-type villa with courtyard (indeed, a 2nd-century well on the site is probably the largest stone-lined well in Roman Britain and has produced a wealth of environmental and other evidence) [1]. The site was rediscovered by workmen digging for limestone in 1781 [1].

row.name: British Camp
row.description: British Camp is an Iron Age hill fort located at the top of Herefordshire Beacon in the Malvern Hills [1]. The fort is thought to have been first constructed in the 2nd century BC [1]. British Camp is composed of extensive earthworks that have been compared to a giant wedding cake [1]. The ditch and counterscarp bank around the entire site covers three hills, although those to north and south are little more than spurs [1]. With a perimeter of 6,800 feet, the defences enclose an area of around 44 acres [1]. The first earthworks were around the base of the central hill otherwise known as the citadel [1]. At least four pre-historic phases of building have so far been identified [1].

row.name: Pocklington Iron Age Burial Ground
row.description: The Pocklington Iron Age burial ground is a prehistoric cemetery discovered in 2014 on the outskirts of Pocklington in the East Riding of Yorkshire [1]. Excavations carried out on an ongoing basis since then, have uncovered more than 160 skeletons and more than 70 square barrows thought to date to the Middle Iron Age that are attributed to the Arras culture, an ancient British culture of East Yorkshire [1]. A variety of grave goods have been found along with the human remains, including weapons, beads, pots, and a rare chariot burial [1]. In one barrow the remains of a warrior were found [1]. He had been placed on top of his shield – the first example of a shield burial to have been found in Britain [1]. In 2016, the well-preserved remains of another warrior aged between 17 and 23 years old were discovered [1]. A broken sword had been placed by his side, which had probably been broken as part of a funeral ritual [1]. The skeleton also was interred with five spears that had been used ritually to pierce the warrior's body [1].

row.name: Ras il-Wardija
row.description: Ras il-Wardija is a promontory in the limits of San Lawrenz, on the southwest coast of Gozo [1]. It contains the remains of a Punic-Roman sanctuary, which was excavated by Italian archaeologists in the 1960s [1]. Ras il-Wardija was probably first inhabited in the Bronze Age, in around 1500 BC [1]. Around the 3rd century BC, during the Punic period, a religious complex (probably a nymphaeum) was established in the area [1]. The site remained in use throughout the Roman period [1]. Carved crosses on the walls suggest that the site eventually became a Christian place of worship [1]. The site remained in use until around the 4th century AD [1]. The site was first excavated by the Missione Archaeologica Italiana a Malta between 1964 and 1967 [1].

row.name: Quinkan Rock Art
row.description: Quinkan rock art refers to a large body of locally, nationally and internationally significant Aboriginal rock art in Australia of a style characterised by their unique representations of "Quinkans" (an Aboriginal mythological being, often spelt "Quinkin"), found among the sandstone escarpments around the small town of Laura, Queensland [1]. Quinkan Country was inscribed on the Australian National Heritage List on 10 November 2018 [1]. The Australian Heritage Commission's 1980 entry on the register of the national estate describes the Quinkan rock art as being located across 230,000 hectares of rugged sandstone plateaux and escarpments 4 km south east of Laura and 50 km west of Cooktown [1]. The paintings are generally large and well preserved, and engravings of great antiquity occur [1]. Engravings of both figurative and abstract styles are found throughout Quinkan country [1].

row.name: Boswens Menhir
row.description: Boswens Menhir, also known as Boswens standing stone, or the Long Stone, is a standing stone 3 kilometres northeast of St Just in Penwith, in Cornwall [1]. The stone lies to the west of Boswens Common [1]. It is one of many standing stones in Penwith [1]. It is 1.5 km east of Tregeseal stone circle, and about 1 km south of Chûn Quoit [1]. The stone is of rectangular section measuring 0.7 metres by 0.9 metres, and is 2.4 metres high [1]. The front face is symmetrical; at the back there are two steps which reduce the width by half [1]. In 1754 William Borlase illustrated the stone standing in a small low cairn, but by 1861 there was "hardly any trace of cairn" visible [1]. The cairn today is around 0.3 metres high, and is "only just noticeable" [1].

row.name: Begash
row.description: Begash is a Bronze Age archaeological site in the Koksu River valley of historic Zhetysu, southeastern Kazakhstan [1] [2]. Located in piedmont steppes above the Zhalgyzagash River, it was occupied by transhumant pastoralists who mainly herded sheep and goats and likely used the site for winter residence [1]. Burial practices transitioned from cist graves to kurgan burials over time [1] [3].

row.name: Ludgate
row.description: Ludgate was the westernmost gate in London Wall [1]. According to legend, recorded by the Norman-Welsh cleric Geoffrey of Monmouth, Ludgate was named after the ancient British King Lud [1]. Ludgate is believed to have been one of four original gates in the Roman London Wall, work on which started in 190 AD [1]. In February 1554, Ludgate was the final setting of Wyatt's rebellion, when Sir Thomas Wyatt the Younger arrived at the gate with part of his army numbering three or four hundred men [1]. Ludgate was rebuilt in 1586 to the design of William Kerwin; niches in the facade were furnished with statues of Queen Elizabeth I and King Lud with his two sons; these statues replaced medieval ones that had been defaced by Protestant iconoclasts during the reign of King Edward VI [1].

row.name: Trink Hill
row.description: Trink Hill is a 212-metre-high hill that lies between the hamlets of Trink and Cripplesease, near to the village of Nancledra [1]. A Round barrow exists at the summit, an OS Trig point within it [1]. A stone named after the nearby Giew Mine (or Trink Hill menhir) stands on the western slope of the hill [1].

row.name: Wraxall Camp
row.description: Wraxall Camp, or Failand Camp, is a small round earthwork in Somerset [1]. The remains are indistinct and thickly covered by woods, but it appears to have been an Iron Age farmstead, and not a defensive structure [1]. Wraxall Camp is a scheduled monument in the parish of Wraxall and Failand in North Somerset, in an upland region of carboniferous limestone [1]. The site is 1.5 miles east of Wraxall village and 100 metres north of Failand village [1]. It is an Iron Age settlement with a raised oval interior about 40 metres wide on the long axis [1]. Partial excavations in 1928 found sherds of black burnished pottery and a Kimmeridge shale bracelet, typical of rural settlements in the Iron Age [1]. Minor earthworks mark the homes in the interior, which were surrounded by a bank and ditch [1]. The bank, up to 8 metres wide, was made of earth and small stones over natural rock outcrops [1].

row.name: Guitarrero Cave
row.description: Guitarrero Cave is located in the Callejón de Huaylas valley in Yungay Province, in the Ancash region of Peru [1]. Guitarrero Cave has evidence of human use around 8,000 BCE and possibly as early as 10,560 BCE [1]. Some of the earliest cultivated plants in South America have been found in the cave [1].

row.name: Doctor's Gate
row.description: Doctor's Gate is a Roman road in the Derbyshire Peak District of England, which ran between Melandra fort at Glossop and Navio fort at Brough-on-Noe [1]. Doctor's Gate was recorded in 1627 as "Docto Talbotes Gate", named after Dr John Talbot who is attributed with improving the summit section in the late 15th century and 'gate' is derived from the Scandinavian word for road [1]. The route of Doctor's Gate was investigated in the 1970s by Peter Wroe and Peter Mellor [1]. Doctor's Gate Road was assigned the Margary number RR711 by Roman road historian Ivan Donald Margary, who commented that the road was "remarkably direct considering the very difficult country that the route has to traverse" [1].

row.name: Kings Weston Roman Villa
row.description: Kings Weston Roman Villa is located in Lawrence Weston in the north-west of Bristol [1]. The ruins of the Roman villa are a Scheduled Monument that represents a winged corridor design common in Roman Britain [1]. It is notable for retaining original mosaic floors, a hypocaust system, and the only Roman bath suite visible in Bristol [1]. Numismatic evidence, including coins of the Valentinian and Gratian periods (up to AD 381), suggests occupation continued into the late 4th century [1]. The villa was rediscovered in November 1947 during the post-war construction of the Lawrence Weston housing estate [1]. The primary villa was established during Period One (AD 268–270), featuring two wings connected by an open colonnaded porticus and a central court [1]. The villa contains two in situ 4th-century mosaics [1].

row.name: Raw Dykes
row.description: Raw Dykes is a Roman earthwork and scheduled monument in Leicester [1]. The monument consists of two parallel banks up to 20 metres apart, with an excavated channel running between them [1]. A stretch 110 metres long survives, but originally the earthwork was at least 550 metres in length [1]. The first written reference to the earthwork occurs in the borough of Leicester's accounts from 1322 [1]. During the English Civil War, Royalist soldiers used part of the earthwork as an artillery emplacement; it also appears on several 18th- and 19th-century maps [1]. Since the early modern period its length has been greatly shortened by the expansion of Leicester [1].

row.name: Portingbury Hills
row.description: Portingbury Hills or Portingbury Rings is a hill in Hatfield Forest, Hatfield Broad Oak, Essex [1]. Archaeological excavations were carried out in 1964–1965, with recovered evidence including a small flint blade 4 cm long, animal bones, flints, and charcoal, dated to the Iron Age [1]. The earthworks at Portingbury consist of 3 features; a hill and mound connected by a zig-zag causeway formed by 2 almost parallel ditches to another rectangular enclosure measuring 30 by 21 metres surrounded by a large ditch with a suggested bank up to 11 metres wide [1]. They are located in the northwest of Hatfield Forest in Beggarshall coppice [1]. Archaeologists suggested that the initial ditch surrounding the mound would have been approximately 2 metres in depth suggesting it once had earth ramparts supported by timber [1]. However the earthworks are too small to be a hillfort and are not in a defensible position [1].

row.name: Huaca Casa Rosada
row.description: Huaca Casa Rosada is an archaeological site located in San Miguel District, in Lima, Peru [1]. The site presents evidence of human occupation from the Intermediate period to the Inca period and remains from the Spanish colonial and Republican periods [1]. The archaeological site consists of a square-shaped structure of approximately 36 meters on each side and around 3 to 4 meters high, formed by rammed earth and adobe to build a platform [1]. The huaca has structures with big adobes that were filled with earth and wall fragments to serve as the base for the house of Republican period, known as "Casa Rosada", made with Quincha and wood walls [1]. During the archaeological excavations carried out between 1973 and 1974, by the “Seminario de Arqueología” of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, fragments of turned and glazed pottery, earthenware and imported fine ceramics from the 16th-18th centuries were found [1]. During excavations in the early 2000s, compartments made of rammed earth walls were found at the top of the building, below the Republican house [1].

row.name: Overstone Anglo-Saxon Cemetery
row.description: Overstone Anglo-Saxon cemetery is an Anglo-Saxon place of burial discovered at the Overstone Leys housing development site near the village of Overstone, Northamptonshire [1]. The burial site was found during an archaeological investigation in 2019 [1]. It is the biggest Anglo-Saxon cemetery ever found in Northamptonshire [1]. The 15 hectare site was excavated in 2019 by the Museum of London Archaeology over a 12 month period [1]. Uncovered during the excavation were 154 individual graves and 3000 artefacts [1]. Included in the individual burials were many grave goods, consisting primarily of jewellery and weapons [1]. A group of 22 previously unknown Anglo-Saxon era structures were also found at the site [1]. The assemblage was a combination of sunken-feature buildings and post-built structures [1].

row.name: Niumatou Site
row.description: The Niumatou Site (traditional Chinese: 牛罵頭遺址; simplified Chinese: 牛骂头遗址; pinyin: Niúmàtóu Yízhǐ) is an archaeological site dating from the mid Neolithic period in Qingshui District, Taichung, Taiwan [1]. It is the oldest archaeological site in central Taiwan [1]. Civilizations in the area date to around 4,000 years ago when prehistoric people settled there during the Neolithic age [1]. These cultures left behind stone tools and pottery [1]. Because large numbers of stone hoes were unearthed, archaeologists think that those prehistoric people probably relied largely on farming for food [1]. However, they also hunted and fished to add more variety to their diets [1].

row.name: Balanica
row.description: Balanica is a cave complex, archaeological and palentological site in the City of Niš' municipality of Niška Banja in southeast Serbia [1]. It consists of Velika Balanica and Mala Balanica [1]. The Balanica caves are located within the Sićevo Gorge, some 100 m away from the last houses in the Sićevo village [1]. Balanica caves were discovered in 2002 [1]. In 2006, a hominin hemi-mandible BH-1 was discovered at Mala Balanica [1]. The mandible was excavated in the lower stratigraphic level of the cave, 1.5 m below the artifact bearing level [1]. It was the first hominin specimen in the Central Balkans recovered through controlled excavations with firm stratigraphic context [1]. Remains in Velika Balanica make it one of the oldest localities in Europe where transition from the Lower to Middle Paleolithic is recorded [1].

row.name: Nohmul
row.description: Nohmul is a pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site located on the eastern Yucatán Peninsula, in what is today northern Belize [1]. The site included a large pyramid, about 17 meters tall, built around 250 BC [1]. Nohmul was occupied initially during the Preclassic era of Mesoamerican chronology (c. 350 BC to 250 AD) [1]. By the 5th century, monumental construction at the site had effectively ceased and the site seems to have been largely abandoned save for some scattered rural-domestic activities [1]. After a hiatus in construction activities of several centuries, Nohmul was reoccupied and large-scale building resumed, with maximal activity seen during the Late Classic era (c. 7th–10th centuries) [1]. The site was densely developed and occupied into the 12th century [1]. The site includes about 700 visible mounds ranging from 10 to 30 meters in diameter and from 1 to 5 meters in height [1].

row.name: Blackpatch
row.description: Blackpatch is an archaeological site in West Sussex, England, about 2 miles west of the village of Findon and about 3 miles north-west of Worthing [1]. It is the site of a Neolithic flint mine, and Bronze Age barrows [1]. The flint mine, which was levelled about 1950, is on the south-west slope of Blackpatch Hill [1]. There are more than 64 infilled shafts, diameter up to 6 metres [1]. The shafts and other features at the site were investigated from 1922 to 1932 by John Pull [1]. Seven shafts were excavated [1]. They were up to 3 metres deep; from them, galleries extended up to 8.5 metres, following a single seam of flint [1]. Flint flakes and pottery sherds were found in the infills from the shafts [1].

row.name: Post Track
row.description: The Post Track is an ancient causeway in the valley of the River Brue on the Somerset Levels [1]. It is dated back to around 3838 BCE, making it some 30 years older than the Sweet Track in the same area [1]. Various sections have been scheduled as ancient monuments [1]. The timber trackway was constructed of long ash planks, with lime and hazel posts spaced along three-metre intervals [1]. Some of the wood planks were also reused in the Sweet Track when it was built, making the specific dating more complex [1].

row.name: Punta de Chimino
row.description: Punta de Chimino is a Maya archaeological site in the Petexbatún region of the department of Petén in Guatemala [1]. Occupation at the site dates to the Preclassic and Classic periods of Mesoamerican chronology [1]. The site is located on a peninsula on the western side of Lake Petexbatún [1]. In the Late Classic a series of defensive ditches were excavated across the base of this peninsula in order to fortify the site [1]. The site is one of very few locations in the Pasión drainage to have erected major architecture during the Terminal Classic, including a corbel-vaulted temple, large palace platforms and a very large ballcourt [1]. The neck of the peninsula was fortified with three moats, one of which was 12 metres deep, each moat was topped by a palisaded wall [1]. The area between these moats was used for intensive agriculture and included box gardens divided by crude stone walls [1].

row.name: Langweiler - Archaeological Site
row.description: Langweiler is an archaeological site situated in the Merzbach Valley on the Aldenhovener Plateau of western Germany [1]. Systematic excavations have revealed evidence of 160 houses from eight distinct settlement sites, plus three enclosures and a cemetery, belonging to the period 5300-4900 BC [1]. The site is a key region for understanding the nature of the earliest farming societies in west-central Europe (Bandkeramik era) [1]. Extensive surveys done from 1973 to 1981 contributed to recovery of the largest settlements in the valley before destruction of the area for mining [1]. The settlement at Langweiler 8 lasted over 300 years, with permanent occupation of about 15 houses [1]. The agricultural basis for these Bandkeramik settlements is reconstructed as small-scale cereal cultivation in fixed plots adjacent to the settlements [1]. During the latest stage of the Merzbach Bandkeramik period, special enclosures were constructed which may have been the setting for social or ritual activities by whole communities [1].

row.name: Stravomyti Cave
row.description: Stravomyti Cave is an ancient Minoan cave on Crete [1]. Stravomyti Cave is 400 meters above sea level on Mt. Juktas' southwest slope [1]. Stravomyti Cave first saw use during Neolithic times, as a refuge and burial [1]. During the Early Minoan period, the quality of pottery suggests that people lived in the caves [1]. Thereafter, it was used for storage and worship [1]. The cave may have once been a shrine to a female deity - Artemis, Diktynna or perhaps Eileithyia [1].

row.name: Arbury Hill
row.description: Arbury Hill, at 225 m, is the joint highest point in the English county of Northamptonshire [1]. It is 9 km southwest of the town of Daventry [1]. On the summit of Arbury Hill there are the vestiges of an Iron Age Fort, although its date and origin are disputed [1]. The remains are in the form of a square ditch and embankment about 200 metres across [1]. Although little trace remains of this fort, the outer bank encloses an area of about 12 acres [1]. It is mentioned as one of the boundary marks in a land grant of Edmund the Elder, as being the place where the three parishes of Badby, Dodford and Everdon meet [1].

row.name: Amazmaz
row.description: Amazmaz is an isolated elevation with steep slopes in the western part of the Adrar plateau in Mauritania, 400 km northeast of the capital Nouakchott [1]. At the foot of the hill there are the gueltas of Amazmaz, a chain of ponds, hidden among rocks and surrounded by rushes, but used for thousands of years, as evidenced by the rock paintings on the slopes bordering the waters [1].

row.name: Villa of Lucullus
row.description: The villa of Lucullus was an extensive and sumptuous ancient Roman villa built in the first century BC in Naples by the famous gourmet, general and consul Lucius Licinius Lucullus [1]. The villa was equipped with piers that stretched out into the sea, a very rich library, fish ponds and moray eel farms and lavish gardens with peach trees imported from Persia which for the time were a novelty along with the cherry trees he brought in from Cerasus [1]. At some point after the death of Lucullus (57/56 BC), the villa passed to the Roman emperor; later, under Valentinian III (419-455), it was transformed into a fortress, and since then has been called the castellum Lucullanum, and was the place of exile of Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman Emperor [1]. Remains of the villa, given its enormous area, are visible at several places in the city of Naples [1]. The largest and perhaps most important nucleus is located in the cellar of the Castel dell'Ovo situated on the islet of Megaride, the so-called "hall of columns" derived from the Roman columns still standing [1].

row.name: La Grotte des Fées
row.description: La Grotte des Fées is a cave located in Châtelperron, in the central French department of Allier [1]. The name refers to three caves, of which one is collapsed [1]. The caves are located in the commune of Châtelperron, about 1 km north of the town [1]. Two interlinked caves were first discovered around 1840, perhaps in 1848, during the construction of the railway which used to link the mines from Bert to Dompierre-sur-Besbre [1]. A third cave (today collapsed), was discovered in 1867 by Bailleau [1]. Several thousand flint blades and mammoth tusks of over 2 metres (6 ft 7 in) long were found [1]. The last research, from 1951 to 1954 and in 1962, was led by Henri Delporte and revealed back blades of flint, burins, drills and scrapers [1].

row.name: Altar of the Twelve Gods
row.description: The Altar of the Twelve Gods (also called the Sanctuary of the Twelve Gods), was an important altar and sanctuary at Athens, located in the northwest corner of the Classical Agora [1]. The altar was set up by Pisistratus the Younger, (the grandson of the tyrant Pisistratus) during his archonship [1]. The altar was dismantled c. 267 AD [1]. From at least the 5th century BC, the altar became the zero point from which distances to Athens were calculated [1]. The altar also functioned as a place of supplication and refuge [1]. The exact location of the altar within the Classical Agora, unspecified in ancient sources, was discovered through excavations, in 1891 and 1934, at a site just opposite the Stoa of Zeus, and adjacent to the Panathenaic Way [1]. The Altar's rectangular enclosure or peribolos, was roughly square, 9.5m per side [1]. A parapet wall surrounded a paved enclosure containing a rectangular altar proper, presumably at its center [1].

row.name: Herxheim - Archaeological Site
row.description: The archaeological site of Herxheim was a ritual center and a mass grave formed by people of the Linear Pottery culture in Neolithic Europe [1]. The site dates from between 5300 and 4950 BC [1]. Herxheim was discovered in 1996 on the site of a construction project when locals reported finds of bones, including human skulls [1]. The deposition of the human remains occurred only within the final 50 years of occupation at the site [1]. A detailed study published by the excavators in 2015 estimates that the site contains the scattered remains of more than 1000 individuals [1].

row.name: Azargoshnasp Fire Temple
row.description: Adur Gushnasp was the name of a Zoroastrian sacred fire of the highest grade, which served as one of the three most sacred fires of pre-Islamic Iran; the two others being the Adur Farnbag and Adur Burzen-Mihr [1]. Out of the three, Adur Gushnasp is the only fire whose temple structure has been discovered and for which archaeological, sigillographical, and textual evidence are all available [1]. The temple, constructed by the Sasanian kings, was located in the city of Shiz in Adurbadagan, now present-day Takht-e Soleymān in the West Azerbaijan province [1]. It served as a prominent site of pilgrimage [1]. The fire is not mentioned in early Sasanian sources, and archaeology suggests that the fire was first taken to the site in Adurbadagan in the late 4th or early 5th-century [1]. The fire temple was sacked in 623/4 by Heraclius during the Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628 [1]. The fire continued to burn for a long period in the Islamic era, but persecution eventually increased, and by the late 10th-century, or early 11th-century, the fire had most likely been quenched [1].

row.name: Temple of Proserpina
row.description: The Temple of Proserpina or Temple of Proserpine was a Roman temple in Mtarfa, Malta, an area which was originally a suburb outside the walls of Melite [1]. It was dedicated to Proserpina, goddess of the underworld and renewal [1]. The date of construction is unknown, but it was renovated in the 1st century BC or AD [1]. The ruins of the temple were discovered in 1613, and most of its marble blocks were later used in the decoration of buildings, including Auberge d'Italie and the Castellania in Valletta [1]. The only epigraphic evidence of the temple is the Chrestion inscription, which was discovered among its ruins in 1613 [1]. It records that the temple was already old and was threatening to collapse during the reign of Augustus in the 1st century BC or AD, and it was restored by Chrestion, the procurator of the Maltese Islands [1]. This inscription is the earliest known Latin text that was found in Malta [1]. The temple was built out of marble and its columns were in the Corinthian order [1].

row.name: Wilsford Henge
row.description: Wilsford Henge is the site of a Neolithic henge, west of the village of Wilsford, Wiltshire in the United Kingdom [1]. The monument lies within the Vale of Pewsey, a short distance south of the large henge known as Marden Henge [1]. Wilsford Henge is a broad irregular circular ditch visible only as a cropmark on aerial photographs, on a gently sloping spur of land about 500m south of the River Avon [1]. The internal diameter of the enclosure is around 43 metres and the external diameter is around 62 metres [1]. There is an entrance, 12 metres wide, which faces northeast in the direction of the river [1]. An interior circle of possible post-hole pits has been confirmed by geophysical survey [1]. The site was included in a three-year investigation of the Pewsey Vale, beginning in 2015, by the Department of Archaeology at the University of Reading [1]. Among the discoveries in the 2015 excavations was an early Bronze Age crouched burial of an adolescent child which included sherds of beaker pottery and a collection of necklace beads [1].

row.name: Hammerum Burial Site
row.description: The Hammerum burial site is an archaeological excavation located about 5 km east of Herning, Denmark [1]. The site has been dated to the late Roman Iron Age and contained preserved fabric from graves of that era [1]. In 1993, initial stages of new road development revealed traces of several graves throughout the land slated for construction [1]. Seven graves were discovered upon further excavation [1]. Grave 100, excavated in 2008, contained several subjects of interest: an as yet indeterminable organic substance; remains of human hair arranged in such a design as to indicate a female wearer; and sparse remains of animal hide [1]. In Grave 83, similarly to Grave 100, the only remains of the deceased is a preserved complex coiffure; this, combined with the size of the grave, indicates that the deceased was either a large girl or a young woman [1]. The grave has thus been labelled the Hammerum Girl [1]. The grave contains unusually well-preserved clothing [1].

row.name: Nakhchivan Necropolises
row.description: The Nakhchivan necropolis is an archeological site of the Bronze Age on the northern outskirts of Nakhchivan city [1]. The monument was accidentally discovered in 1968 when earth graves were destroyed during farm work [1]. The surface of the rectangular tombs is covered with stone slabs 1 m long, 0.5 m wide and 0.2–0.3 m thick [1]. The remains of the skeletons are very poorly preserved [1]. Nakhchivan necropolis I is an archeological monument of antiquity near the Nakhchivan necropolis [1]. It was discovered by accident during construction in 1970 [1]. The monument with an area of 1.9 hectares consists of six destroyed tombs [1].

row.name: Navio Roman Fort
row.description: Navio Roman fort overlooks a tight bend of the River Noe at Brough-on-Noe near Hope, Derbyshire [1]. Excavations in the 1930s by Sir Ian Richmond and J.P. Gillam established the locations of the perimeters of successive forts on the same site [1]. Navio fort was originally about 3 acres in size and built of timber and earthworks around 80 CE [1]. It was rebuilt in stone in a rectangular form (about 90 by 105 metres (295 by 344 ft)) around 150 CE from when it was occupied for over 200 years [1]. It was subsequently rebuilt and altered and in use until around 350 CE [1]. Earlier excavations in 1903 by John Garstang uncovered steps into an underground stone-walled chamber below the Principia or headquarters building [1]. The fort guarded the Doctor's Gate route northwest to the larger fort of Melandra [1].

row.name: Kastros
row.description: Kastros is an early Neolithic settlement in Cyprus [1]. Kastros lies at the north-easternmost tip of the Karpas Peninsula, about 4 km north of Apostolos Andreas Monastery [1]. The settlement is situated on a little plateau at the steep flank of the limestone promontory, about halfway between the main plateau of the peninsula and the sea in a very inaccessible location [1]. Between 1970 and 1973 three campaigns of excavations were conducted by a French team headed by Alain Le Brun [1]. The settlement consists of small round or roundish houses [1]. The houses contain a hearth and sometimes container-bins in the floor [1]. The site belongs to the aceramic Neolithic and dates to the 6th Millennium BC [1]. The carbonised remains of einkorn, emmer and some barley have been found [1].

row.name: Konjic Mithraeum
row.description: The Konjic Mithraeum, or Konjički Mithraeum, is a Mithraeum, early 4th century AD temple dedicated to God of the Sun, Mithra, discovered in Konjic, Bosnia and Herzegovina [1]. The remains of the Mithraeum in Konjic were discovered in January 1897, at the banks of river Trešanica, under village Repovci, on the outskirts of Konjic [1]. The Konjic site is atypical as its floor level is at ground level [1]. The mithraic relief of Konjic, carved in gray limestone, is two-sided relief, and it shows a Tauroctony in one side and a ritual meal in the other [1].

row.name: Schalkholz Passage Grave
row.description: The Schalkholz Passage Grave, also known as Schalkholz-Vierth is a megalithic burial site of the Neolithic period and of the Funnelbeaker culture in Vierth, a district of Schalkholz in the province of Schleswig-Holstein in Germany [1]. During the late Bronze Age or early Iron Age, it was used for a secondary burial site and was expanded upon [1]. It has the Sprockhoff number 139 and the site number LA 33 or Heide LA 5 [1]. The grave was archaeologically investigated in 1969 and 1970 and was afterwards moved to the nearby town of Heide [1]. In 2021 it was moved back to Schalkholz [1].

row.name: Ancient Theatre of Makyneia
row.description: A small 4th-3rd century BC theatre at the site of ancient Aitolian Makyneia, located at the Paliokastro site in western Greece [1] [2]. The theatre has a single cuneus with 14 tiers of seats and an arc-shaped orchestra, and may have doubled as a bouleuterion (council house) [2] [3]. Its compact design features seats of honor (proedriae) in the north part of the orchestra, with stone seat-backs for distinguished officials [2] [3]. Analysis shows it was designed using the Doric foot measurement system [1].

row.name: Ackling Dyke
row.description: Ackling Dyke is a section of Roman road in England which runs for 22 miles southwest from Old Sarum (Sorviodunum) to the hill fort at Badbury Rings (Vindocladia) [1]. Much of the road exists as an exceptionally large embankment, up to 50 ft wide and 6 ft high [1]. This is much wider than most Roman roads [1]. This would have been visible from a great distance and must have been intended to impress the native population, as it was unnecessary from an engineering viewpoint [1]. It provided a rapid transit route for soldiers across Cranborne Chase [1]. In addition, in places the road cuts straight through prehistoric earthworks and barrows, showing the Roman attitude to the existing British social structure as well as proving to early antiquaries that barrows preceded the Roman period [1]. At Bokerley Junction it cuts through both Bokerley Dyke and Grim's Ditch before being overlaid by a turnpike, now the A354 [1]. A series of watchtower sites have been identified along the route [1].

row.name: El Salt
row.description: El Salt is an archaeological site from the Middle Paleolithic near Alcoy, in the Spanish Province of Alicante, which was frequented by groups of archaic humans for thousands of years [1]. Scientists have found evidence of Neanderthal settlements, including fire pits and flint tools, dating back at least 50,000 years, including six teeth; they disappeared from the site and possibly the Iberian Peninsula some 45,000 years ago [1]. In 2014, the then-oldest known human coprolites were discovered at the site, which revealed that Neanderthals' diets included plants [1]. El Salt is located close to the confluence of the Polop and Barxell rivers [1]. It is an open-air rock shelter at 680 (or 700) meters above sea level, one of several site clusters in the plain of Valencia that give evidence of "significant levels of mobility across extended territories" by population groups [1]. The site has a 6.3 meters thick stratified deposit, at the bottom of a limestone wall, 38 meters high [1]. Thermoluminescence dating indicated its age is between 60.7 ± 8.9 and 45.2 ± 3.4 Ka [1].

row.name: Arqueológico El Puente Park
row.description: El Puente, or the Parque Arqueológico El Puente, is a Maya archaeological site in the department of Copán in Honduras [1]. The city of El Puente became a tributary to the nearby city of Copán between the 6th and 9th centuries AD [1]. The site contains more than 200 structures that include tombs, religious structures, and living quarters, but only a few have been excavated, including a large Maya step pyramid [1]. El Puente is located in the Florida Valley in the municipality of La Jigua, 11 kilometres to the north of the Honduran town of La Entrada [1]. El Puente appears to have been first settled around the middle of the 6th century AD fairly late in the Mesoamerican timescale and occupation at the site did not last very long [1]. The site was a regional centre during the Late Classic period when it remained closely allied with the great city of Copán [1]. Structure 1 is the tallest building at El Puente, measuring 12 metres tall [1].

row.name: Ballykeel Dolmen
row.description: Ballykeel Dolmen is a Neolithic tripod portal tomb and a State Care Historic Monument at the foot of the western flank of Slieve Gullion in Northern Ireland [1]. It is located above a tributary of the Forkhill river, in the Newry, Mourne and Down District Council area [1]. The dolmen sits at the southern end of a large cairn, of approximately 30x10 metres, the north end of which also contains a cist [1]. Its three metre long capstone, with a notable notch similar to that of Legananny Dolmen, had previously fallen, but was re-set during excavations in 1963 [1]. The granite capstone is balanced on the tips of the three portal stones [1]. Excavations of the chamber revealed different types of pottery, including three highly decorated "Ballyalton" bowls, and the cist contained several hundred sherds of Neolithic pottery, a javelin head, and three flint flakes [1].

row.name: Peyre-Brune
row.description: Peyre-Brune is a Neolithic dolmen situated near Saint-Aquilin in the department of the Dordogne [1]. The dolmen Peyre-Brune is situated next to a forest track leading from Seyssac, a little hamlet in the commune of Saint-Aquilin, to Segonzac [1]. The dolmen is completely surrounded by woods and is positioned on a topographic high at about 200 meters above sea level [1]. The rectangular, one-chambered dolmen is about 2.75 meters long and 2 meters wide, its long axis is oriented towards the south-east [1]. The dolmen was a burial tomb of a local chieftain [1]. Analyses showed that the defunct was not incinerated [1]. Peyre-Brune is one of the very few megalithic monuments in this region, that can be attributed to a local culture [1].

row.name: Castle Ring
row.description: Castle Ring is an Iron Age hill fort, situated high up on the southern edge of Cannock Chase, Staffordshire [1]. It is the highest point on The Chase with an elevation of 242 metres [1]. It is near the village of Cannock Wood, south of Rugeley and north of Burntwood [1]. Castle Ring is thought to have first been occupied c. 500 BCE by an Ancient British tribe named the Cornovii [1]. It was abandoned c. 43 CE as a consequence of Romans occupying the area [1]. Apart from perimeter earthworks, little remains visible [1]. Parts of the ground in the ring appear to have been ploughed, but there is no consensus as to whether this was carried out in prehistoric times, or in the medieval period, when a hunting lodge was also built in the ring [1]. The remains of this lodge are still visible [1].

row.name: Yarnbury Castle
row.description: Yarnbury Castle is the site of a multiphase, multivallate Iron Age hillfort near the village of Steeple Langford, Wiltshire [1]. The site covers an area of 28.5 acres, and was extensively surveyed and investigated by the Royal Commission on the Historical Monuments of England in 1991, with finds of Iron Age and Romano-British pottery, Iron Age and Roman coins, and burials of human remains [1]. There is much evidence of prolonged and extensive settlement of the site, including evidence of around 130 structures of various sizes, most probably representing a mix of round houses, pits, and other features [1]. It was designated as a scheduled monument in 1925 [1]. The earthworks at Yarnbury consist of three ramparts with outer ditches [1]. In the centre of the hillfort lies an earlier and smaller single banked enclosure of 5.2 ha in area [1]. The main earthworks are thought to date from around 100 BC, with the earlier inner circuit being from about 300 BC, according to pottery finds from early Iron Age through to Romano-British, including Samian of around 160 AD [1].

row.name: Tikra
row.description: Tikra is an archaeological site in Peru [1]. It was declared a National Cultural Heritage by Resolución Directoral No. 952/INC on September 20, 2001 [1]. The site consists of circular buildings and square or rectangular burial towers [1]. Tikra is situated in the Huánuco Region, Lauricocha Province, Jesús District [1]. It lies on the slopes of Pitaq Mach'ay northeast of Jesús [1].

row.name: Zacpeten
row.description: Zacpeten is a pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site in the northern Petén Department of Guatemala [1]. The site of Zacpeten occupies a peninsula on Lake Salpeten in the Petén Department of northern Guatemala [1]. The site was sporadically inhabited by the Maya since its initial settlement during the Middle Preclassic (1000 – 300 BC) [1]. After abandonment during Late Preclassic and Early Classic, the site was resettled from the Late to Terminal Classic (AD 600 – 950) [1]. Abandoned again, it was reoccupied in the Late Postclassic by the Maya peoples who survived the Classic Maya collapse and migrated from Mayapan in Yucatán after the collapse of the city in the fifteenth century [1]. These people, the Kowoj Maya, brought their distinctive pottery and constructed typical Mayapan temple assemblages with a raised shrine lying at a right angle to a western facing temple rather than facing it, a very different pattern to ceremonial architecture outside central Peten [1]. This civilisation flourished and remained independent of Spanish domination until late into the 17th century, usually recorded as 1697 [1].

row.name: Woodchester Roman Villa
row.description: Woodchester Roman Villa was situated at Woodchester near Stroud in the English county of Gloucestershire [1]. It is one of many Roman villas discovered in Gloucestershire and was occupied between the early 2nd and late 4th centuries AD [1]. There is now nothing visible of the villa above ground and the site is occupied by a later churchyard [1]. The villa's most famous feature is the Orpheus mosaic, the second largest of its kind in Europe and one of the most intricate [1]. It dates to c. AD 325 and was re-discovered by Gloucestershire-born antiquarian Samuel Lysons in 1793 [1]. It has been uncovered seven times since 1880, the last time in 1973, but there are no plans to reveal it again [1]. It depicts Orpheus charming all forms of life with his lyre and has been praised for its accuracy and beauty [1].

row.name: Nyaung-gan
row.description: Nyaung-gan is a Bronze Age cemetery in central Myanmar, and was the first site in Myanmar to have artefacts dating to the Bronze Age [1]. The ancient cemetery is located south of Nyaung-gan village in central Myanmar, 120 km northwest of Mandalay [1]. The cemetery has an area of 75 m by 180 m (13,500 m2) and sits at an elevation of 107 m [1]. A majority of the burials were aligned with the head pointing north, with a few exceptions where they were buried pointing south [1]. Of the 43 individuals found 36 were adults and seven were infants or children [1]. Items that were collected at this site include bronze tools, both animal and human bones, pottery and stone tools [1].

row.name: Río Azul
row.description: Río Azul is an archaeological site of the Pre-Columbian Maya civilization [1]. It is the most important site in the Río Azul National Park in the Petén Department of northern Guatemala [1]. Río Azul is situated to the southeast of the Azul river and its apogee dates to the Early Classic period (c. AD 250–600) [1]. In the late 4th century AD Río Azul was dominated by the city of Tikal and its great central Mexican ally Teotihuacan [1]. The Teotihuacan warlord Siyaj K'ak' is mentioned in an inscription at Río Azul dated to AD 393 [1]. Río Azul possesses nine major architectural groups in its site core, each including an elite residential complex and its associated funerary pyramids [1]. The site is known for a number of ornate tombs, some of which are corbel-vaulted [1].

row.name: Battlegore Burial Chamber
row.description: Battlegore Burial Chamber is a Bronze Age burial chamber located in Williton, Somerset [1]. It is composed of three round barrows and possibly a long, chambered barrow [1]. The site was excavated in 1931 by George Gray [1]. The most northernly of the barrows is around 18 metres in diameter and 1 metre high [1]. Neolithic pottery and flint artifacts have been found at this site [1]. Archaeologists also found bronze items, including a "knife dagger", a broken dagger, a rapier, a spearhead, and a winged axe [1]. A field of Mesolithic flint artifacts has been found to the north of Battlegore [1].

row.name: Simanya Cave
row.description: Simanya Cave or Great Simanya Cave is a cave in the Sant Llorenç del Munt massif located in the municipality of Sant Llorenç Savall, in Vallès Occidental [1]. It has a route of 372 m and a gradient of 8 m [1]. Between 1929 and 1930, archaeological surveys were carried out led by Pau Codina, in which a large amount of pottery was found from the Chalcolithic [1]. In 1911, ceramics from the Chalcolithic were discovered [1].

row.name: Folkestone Roman Villa
row.description: Folkestone Roman Villa, also referred to as the East Bay Site, is a villa built during the Roman Occupation of Britain, and is located in East Wear Bay near the port town of Folkestone, in Kent [1]. The villa is situated on a cliff top overlooking the English Channel [1]. The villa was built around A. D. 75, and was almost certainly built within the confines of a preexisting Iron Age settlement [1]. The villa was rebuilt and expanded in probably the second century A. D., this time as a more substantial structure with mosaics, a bath-house, and a second block, possibly connected by a courtyard [1]. The villa was abandoned sometime in the third century, though archeological evidence suggests that it was briefly reoccupied in the fourth century [1]. Remains beneath the Roman villa suggest that querns, or stones used to grind cereal crops into flour, were produced here during the Iron Age on an almost industrial scale [1].

row.name: Barry Troglodyte Village
row.description: The Barry Troglodyte Village is an archaeological site near Bollène, northwestern Vaucluse [1]. It is located on a forested hill that overlooks the Rhône valley [1]. A group of caves and stone buildings comprise an ancient village that is historically interesting because it was inhabited continuously from the neolithic until the early 20th century [1]. Most remaining buildings date from the 17th until the 19th century, including a chapel from 1706 that was partly built in a cave [1].

row.name: Kanichi
row.description: Kanichi is an archaeological site in Peru [1]. Kanichi lies in the Ayacucho Region, Lucanas Province, Carmen Salcedo District [1]. The archaeological complex, which is about 200,000 square meters, was influenced by the Wari and Chanka cultures [1]. The complex includes a variety of buildings including Chullpas, religious and ceremonial buildings, service centers, and a water system of wells and springs [1].

row.name: Gonio Fortress
row.description: Gonio is a Roman fortification in Adjara, Georgia, on the Black Sea, 15 km south of Batumi, at the mouth of the Chorokhi river [1]. The oldest reference to the fortress is by Pliny the Elder in the Natural History (1st century AD) [1]. In the 2nd century AD it was a well-fortified Roman city within Colchis [1]. The town was also known for its theatre and hippodrome [1]. Procopius, writing in the 6th century, speaks of the remains of its public buildings as proving that it was once a place of some importance [1]. It later came under Byzantine influence [1]. In 1547, Gonio was taken by the Ottoman Empire, who held it until 1878, when, via the San-Stefano Treaty, Adjara became part of the Russian Empire [1]. The fortress is rectangular, and was built with four gates and 22 towers along the circuit of walls enclosing the site; 18 of the towers still survive [1].

row.card: At the mouth of the Chorokhi river on the Black Sea, the Roman walls of Gonio Fortress still keep 18 of their 22 towers. Its oldest mention comes from Pliny the Elder, in the 1st century AD.

row.name: Leskernick Hill
row.description: Leskernick Hill is on Bodmin Moor in Cornwall [1]. It is 329m high and has grid reference SX183803 [1]. On the south and western slopes of Leskernick Hill are 2 Bronze Age settlements, with associated field enclosures, small cairns, a cist and a propped stone [1]. Between 1995 and 1999, Barbara Bender, Sue Hamilton and Christopher Tilley directed a changing group of UCL students in the landscape investigation of the late Neolithic and Bronze Age archaeological sites on, and near, Leskernick Hill, with associated archaeological excavations [1].
