row.old_value: Largest Anglo-Saxon cemetery in Northamptonshire -- 15 hectares excavated in 2019. Over 160 skeletons and 70 square barrows of the Arras culture, with a range of grave goods.
row.new_value: Overstone Anglo-Saxon cemetery is an Anglo-Saxon place of burial discovered at the Overstone Leys housing development site near the village of Overstone, Northamptonshire.

row.old_value: A stone circle originally 13.7 metres across, now reduced from seven stones to four. Cup marks carved into one surviving stone hint at ritual significance lost to time.
row.new_value: In 1877, William Greenwell and Llewellynn Jewitt excavated at the site, and in the late 1930s the Derbyshire Archaeological Society set two of the orthostats standing again.

row.old_value: Ceremonial centre active 1200-800 BC during the Kishka Pata Period in the Ayacucho Valley. One of the region's earliest known ritual sites - organised ceremonial activity five centuries before Chavin.
A Roman gate in London's defensive wall from the 3rd century AD, with two circular towers flanking the road to Colchester. It stood for over 1,400 years before demolition.
row.new_value: A 1585 sketch of Aldgate's north tower reveals an interior room of approximately 16 by 14 foot; its southern sibling probably had similar dimensions.

row.old_value: Chambered long barrow 24 m long and 13 m wide at the east end, built 3400–2400 BC near Abbotsbury. Early 19th-century excavations recovered human bones and pottery fragments.
row.new_value: The Grey Mare and her Colts is a megalithic chambered long barrow located near Abbotsbury in Dorset.

row.old_value: 16-stone axial circle 8 metres in diameter, two stone rows, and a relocated ogham stone -- the full megalithic repertoire on a single County Cork site. The central slab may have served as an altar.
row.new_value: Carrigagulla is a megalithic complex 2.9 km north-east of Ballinagree, County Cork. Carrigagulla A is an 8-metre-diameter stone circle consisting of 16 standing stones circling a central slab.

row.old_value: 27 BC triumphal arch flanked by fluted Corinthian columns. Four carved shields display Jupiter, Apollo, Neptune, and Roma — one of Rome’s oldest surviving arches, still standing after two millennia.
row.new_value: During the 12th century, the arch contained the home of a local noble family and in 1318 a small fortification was built inside it, designed for a corps of crossbowmen.

row.old_value: A 4th-century BC winery with about 500 square metres of floor space, used for a century before fire destroyed it. The remains reveal ancient grape-pressing methods.
row.new_value: The building was erected in the middle of the 4th century BC and used until the beginning of the 3rd century BC; then it was destroyed by a fire and abandoned by its inhabitants.

row.old_value: Standing stone 2.4 metres high with a rectangular cross-section; the back face has two carved steps -- unusual detail absent from most Penwith menhirs. Located 3 km northeast of St Just in Cornwall.
Human remains carbon-dated to 10,610 BC found here; use continued from 8000 BC onward. Cultivated beans and peppers from this cave document early plant domestication in the Americas.
row.new_value: Guitarrero Cave has evidence of human use around 8,000 BCE and possibly as early as 10,560 BCE.

row.old_value: Neolithic flint mine with over 64 infilled shafts, each up to 6 metres across, on a West Sussex hillside. Levelled around 1950, Bronze Age barrows share the same scheduled site.
row.new_value: The flint mine, which was levelled about 1950, is on the south-west slope of Blackpatch Hill.

row.old_value: Rock art from 10,000-4500 BC on an isolated elevation in what is now desert. The paintings depict animals from a greener Sahara that no longer exists.
8000 BC Neolithic settlement at the tip of the Karpasia Peninsula. Three French campaigns between 1970 and 1973 revealed one of the earliest known human habitations on a limestone promontory.
row.new_value: Kastros lies at the north-easternmost tip of the Karpas Peninsula, about 4 km north of Apostolos Andreas Monastery.

row.old_value: 2nd-4th century AD Mithraic temple in the Neretva valley, atypical because its floor sits at ground level rather than underground. The Konjic site shows how the Mithra cult spread via Roman soldiers.
row.new_value: The remains of the Mithraeum in Konjic were discovered in January 1897, at the banks of river Trešanica, under village Repovci, on the outskirts of Konjic.

row.old_value: A Roman road with an embankment up to 15 metres wide and 1.8 metres high, running 35 km across the landscape. Roman engineers overbuilt this stretch for unknown reasons.
row.new_value: Much of the road exists as an exceptionally large embankment, up to 50 ft wide and 6 ft high.

row.old_value: A Middle Paleolithic site where Neanderthals camped for thousands of years. In 2014, the oldest known human coprolites were found here — direct evidence of Neanderthal diet.
row.new_value: El Salt is an archaeological site from the Middle Paleolithic near Alcoy which was frequented by groups of archaic humans for thousands of years.

row.old_value: A Neolithic tripod portal tomb balanced on three upright stones. The capstone looks precarious but has survived in this position for over 5,000 years.
row.new_value: The dolmen sits at the southern end of a large cairn, of approximately 30x10 metres, the north end of which also contains a cist.

row.old_value: A Neolithic dolmen near Saint-Aquilin in the Dordogne, dated to around 2400 BC. Its name joins the Occitan peyre ('stone') and the word for brown, a nod to the mottled colour of the local rock.
row.new_value: Peyre-Brune is a Neolithic dolmen situated near Saint-Aquilin in the department of the Dordogne.

row.old_value: Hillfort at 242 metres -- the highest point on Cannock Chase in Staffordshire. The original entrance gap, banks, and ditch are still clearly visible along the southern escarpment edge.
row.new_value: Castle Ring is an Iron Age hill fort, situated high up on the southern edge of Cannock Chase, Staffordshire.

row.old_value: Maya city active 1000 BC-950 AD, one of few communities that maintained independence into early Spanish colonial rule. Zacpeten's groups are enclosed by a defensive wall with two parapets and a moat.
row.new_value: The site was sporadically inhabited by the Maya since its initial settlement during the Middle Preclassic.

row.old_value: Mentioned by Pliny the Elder and linked to the myth of Medea, this Roman Black Sea fortress dates from the early centuries AD. Gold, silver, and jeweled artifacts were recovered from its layers.
row.new_value: The fortress is rectangular, and was built with four gates and 22 towers along the circuit of walls enclosing the site; 18 of the towers still survive.

row.old_value: A karst cave with Mousterian tools and a Neanderthal molar, dating occupation back 50,000 years. The cave has two levels with a large terrace at the entrance.
row.new_value: In a series of excavations between 1984 and 1985 Palaeolithic stone artifacts and Pleistocene faunal remains were uncovered.

row.old_value: A ceremonial mound complex spanning 2,000 years of coastal occupation. The Huaca de los Reyes features dramatic adobe reliefs of fanged jaguar faces.
row.new_value: The archaeological complex of Caballo Muerto features stone and adobe constructions, with mud used as mortar.

row.old_value: A Neolithic dolmen where the remains of 56 people were found during excavation. Its massive capstone measures about 3 metres across and rests at ground level on one end.
row.new_value: The remains of fifty-six people who were buried here have been found during excavations.

row.old_value: A jawbone unearthed here — BH-1 — is between 397,000 and 525,000 years old, making it the easternmost Middle Pleistocene human fossil in Europe. Neanderthal teeth also found in 2022.
row.new_value: Remains in Velika Balanica make it one of the oldest localities in Europe where transition from the Lower to Middle Paleolithic is recorded.

row.old_value: Around 1000 AD, Kanichi blended Wari and Chanka influences into one complex: chullpas, ceremonial buildings, service centres, and a water system of wells and springs at 4,000+ metres.

row.old_value: A hillfort occupied in two phases: an early Iron Age ring fort from ~800 BC and a later promontory fort from ~300 BC. Folklore calls the hill a giant's grave.
row.new_value: On a chalk spur of the South Downs, the Iron Age hillfort of Torberry Hill held infilled storage pits and yielded a curry comb, two knives, an iron spearhead and a horn weaving-comb.

row.old_value: A 4th-century gateway added through Hadrian's Wall where a burn flows beneath via a culvert. One of the rare later additions that pierced the wall.
row.new_value: Where Hadrian's Wall crosses the Knag Burn, east of Housesteads, one lane ran between guard-chambers with a gate at each end: the Knag Burn Gateway, a two-stage passage through the wall.

row.old_value: The remains of fifty-six people who were buried here have been found during excavations.
row.new_value: Near Benllech on Anglesey, the massive capstone of the Neolithic Pant-y-Saer Burial Chamber rests one end on the ground. Excavations found the remains of fifty-six people buried here.

row.old_value: An underground chamber dug 6 metres into a large mound around 2,000 years ago. Narrow steps spiral down into a rock-cut space whose purpose — ritual, storage, or something else — remains unknown.
row.new_value: Inside a large mound on Orkney, stone steps turn back on themselves and descend to the Iron Age chamber of Mine Howe, 6 meters deep: only about 1.3 metres across, with a corbelled roof.

row.old_value: Active 1st–4th centuries AD near Torres Novas, this villa takes its name from a mosaic pavement whose inscription remains untranslated. Excavation in 1962 recovered hundreds of coins and bronzes.
row.new_value: Among the rural suburbs of Torres Novas lie the Roman Ruins of Villa Cardillio. In 1932, Jalhay and Afonso do Paço began to investigate its grounds and catalogue what had been built there.

row.old_value: During the 12th century, the arch contained the home of a local noble family and in 1318 a small fortification was built inside it, designed for a corps of crossbowmen.
row.new_value: Raised in Aosta in 25 BC to mark Rome's victory over the Salassi, the Arch of Augustus later held the home of a local noble family and, in 1318, a small fort built inside it for crossbowmen.

row.old_value: Radiocarbon dates suggest presence here 22,200 to 14,700 years ago -- among the earliest in South America, though disputed. Part of the Ayacucho cave complex alongside Jaya Machay, the 'pepper cave'.
row.new_value: Pikimachay, a cave in the Ayacucho Valley, yielded some of the oldest plant remains in Peru, including an 11,000-year-old bottle gourd. Later layers held fishtail points, manos and metates.
In 1754 William Borlase drew Boswens Menhir standing in a small low cairn. The stone still rises 2.4 metres in Penwith, Cornwall, but its cairn is now only just noticeable.

row.old_value: An adobe platform pyramid about 36 metres square, with occupations from the Moche period through the Inca conquest. Built from rammed earth and sun-dried brick.
row.new_value: In Lima's San Miguel District, Huaca Casa Rosada rises as a platform of rammed earth and adobe, approximately 36 meters on each side, that became the base of a Republican-period house.

row.old_value: Overstone Anglo-Saxon cemetery is an Anglo-Saxon place of burial discovered at the Overstone Leys housing development site near the village of Overstone, Northamptonshire.
row.new_value: Found in 2019 near Overstone, the Overstone Anglo-Saxon Cemetery held 154 graves, 3000 artefacts and 22 previously unknown structures, its burials rich in jewellery and weapons.

row.old_value: Remains in Velika Balanica make it one of the oldest localities in Europe where transition from the Lower to Middle Paleolithic is recorded.
row.new_value: In 2006 the Balanica caves gave up half a hominin jaw, the first hominin specimen in the Central Balkans recovered through controlled excavations with firm stratigraphic context.

row.old_value: 5300-4900 BC Bandkeramik farming landscape in the Merzbach Valley. Langweiler revealed 160 houses across eight settlement sites, three enclosures, and a cemetery, a window into Europe's first farmers.
row.new_value: In the Merzbach Valley, Langweiler revealed 160 houses, enclosures and a cemetery of the earliest farming societies in west-central Europe, from 5300-4900 BC, before mining destroyed it.

row.old_value: At 225 metres — the joint highest point in Northamptonshire — this summit hillfort enclosed about 4.9 hectares within a square ditch and embankment roughly 200 metres across.
row.new_value: On the summit of Arbury Hill, the joint highest point in Northamptonshire, lie the vestiges of an Iron Age fort whose date and origin are disputed: a square ditch about 200 metres across.
At the foot of Amazmaz, on the Adrar plateau, a chain of ponds hides among rocks and rushes, and rock paintings on the slopes show the waters were used for thousands of years.

row.old_value: 2nd millennium BC. Bronze Age rectangular tombs at Nakhchivan, covered in stone slabs 1 m long, oriented north to south. Excavations found pottery, bronze ornaments, and the bones of the interred.
row.new_value: At the Nakhchivan Necropolises, farm work in 1968 destroyed earth graves and revealed Bronze Age rectangular tombs covered with stone slabs 1 m long, their skeletons very poorly preserved.

row.old_value: A Roman auxiliary fort guarding a bend of the River Noe from the 1st to 4th century AD. A civilian settlement grew up around it, as happened at forts across Britannia.
row.new_value: Above a tight bend of the River Noe, Navio Roman Fort guarded the Doctor's Gate route. Excavations in 1903 uncovered steps down to an underground stone-walled chamber below its headquarters.

row.old_value: Kastros lies at the north-easternmost tip of the Karpas Peninsula, about 4 km north of Apostolos Andreas Monastery.
row.new_value: On a little plateau on the steep flank of a limestone promontory, in a very inaccessible spot, Kastros held small round houses with hearths and the carbonised remains of einkorn and emmer.

row.old_value: A Roman villa whose Orpheus mosaic is the second largest in Europe, dating to ~325 AD. The mosaic is now buried under a churchyard, only uncovered for rare public viewings.
row.new_value: Nothing of Woodchester Roman Villa is visible above ground, yet its Orpheus mosaic, the second largest of its kind in Europe, shows Orpheus charming all forms of life with his lyre.

row.old_value: A Roman villa perched on a clifftop with views across the Channel to the French coast. Human activity at the site goes back thousands of years before the Romans arrived.
row.new_value: On a cliff top above the English Channel, Folkestone Roman Villa rose around A. D. 75. Remains beneath it suggest Iron Age querns, grinding stones, were made on an almost industrial scale.

row.old_value: A temple complex from 1800 BC with massive mound platforms and human-sized sculpted heads depicting deities. Large crowds gathered here for ceremonies long before the Inca existed.
row.new_value: Large polychrome figures are a striking feature of Mojeque in northern Peru, whose main mound is a stepped pyramid of at least six platforms, about 30 m in height and almost quadrangular.

row.old_value: A Roman fortress named after Mars, the god of war, guarding a mountain pass. It grew important enough to become a bishopric in the province of Dacia Ripensis.
row.new_value: Named after Mars, Roman god of war, the garrison of Castra Martis guarded the road through the Vrashka Chuka pass. In 408 the Huns under Uldin took it, apparently by treachery.

row.old_value: The building was erected in the middle of the 4th century BC and used until the beginning of the 3rd century BC; then it was destroyed by a fire and abandoned by its inhabitants.
row.new_value: On the plain of Leivithra lies Kompoloi, an ancient winery of 17 rooms built on a vineyard. Its wine was stored in 32 clay pithoi buried in the ground, until a fire destroyed the building.

row.old_value: Discovered 2014 near Pocklington -- over 160 skeletons and 70 square barrows of the Arras culture, 8th-3rd century BC. The largest Iron Age cemetery in the East Riding, with rich grave goods.
row.new_value: At the Pocklington Iron Age Burial Ground, a warrior lay on his shield, the first shield burial found in Britain, while another was pierced by five spears beside a broken sword.

row.old_value: A Roman villa discovered during 1947 housing construction. Visitors can see the only exposed Roman mosaic pavement in the entire city.
row.new_value: Rediscovered in November 1947 as a housing estate went up, Kings Weston Roman Villa retains its original mosaic floors, a hypocaust and the only Roman bath suite visible in Bristol.

row.old_value: The oldest archaeological site in the central part of the island, with habitation from around 4,000 years ago. Neolithic people here knew agriculture and lived in settled communities.
row.new_value: Around 4,000 years ago Neolithic settlers came to the Niumatou Site, the oldest in central Taiwan. They left pottery and so many stone hoes that they probably relied largely on farming.

row.old_value: Built 3838 BC on the Somerset Levels -- about 30 years older than the Sweet Track. Long ash planks on hazel and lime posts at 3-m intervals carried Neolithic travellers across a waterlogged landscape.
row.new_value: In the valley of the River Brue lies the Post Track, a causeway of long ash planks and lime and hazel posts, dated to around 3838 BCE: some 30 years older than the Sweet Track.

row.old_value: Neolithic henge in Wiltshire's Vale of Pewsey, known only from aerial cropmarks - a broad circular ditch near the River Avon. Positioned south of the massive Marden Henge in a dense ritual landscape.
row.new_value: Seen only as a cropmark from the air, Wilsford Henge gave up an early Bronze Age crouched burial of an adolescent child, with beaker sherds and necklace beads, in the 2015 excavations.

row.old_value: Funnelbeaker culture passage grave, built 3500–2800 BC. Reused in the Bronze or Iron Age, excavated in 1969–70, then physically relocated to its current site for long-term preservation.
row.new_value: A Neolithic burial of the Funnelbeaker culture, the Schalkholz Passage Grave was archaeologically investigated in 1969 and 1970, then moved to Heide. In 2021 it went back to Schalkholz.

row.old_value: The site was sporadically inhabited by the Maya since its initial settlement during the Middle Preclassic.
row.new_value: On a peninsula in Lake Salpeten, Zacpeten was abandoned and resettled more than once. Then the Kowoj Maya came from Mayapan and stayed free of Spanish rule until late into the 17th century.

row.old_value: The archaeological complex, which is about 200,000 square meters, was influenced by the Wari and Chanka cultures.
row.new_value: Influenced by the Wari and Chanka cultures, Kanichi spreads over about 200,000 square meters in Ayacucho, with chullpas, ceremonial buildings and a water system of wells and springs.

row.old_value: In 1877, William Greenwell and Llewellynn Jewitt excavated at the site, and in the late 1930s the Derbyshire Archaeological Society set two of the orthostats standing again.
row.new_value: On Harthill Moor stand the Grey Ladies of Nine Stones Close, a stone circle whose purpose is unknown. Its ring had seven stones in the mid-19th century; four remain.

row.old_value: 1st–5th century AD. Linked Calleva Atrebatum (Silchester) to Aquae Sulis (Bath) — a military highway later used by medieval drovers. Its earthwork ghost survives as part of the Wansdyke.
row.new_value: Drovers, merchants and travellers used the Roman Road from Silchester to Bath, from Calleva Atrebatum to Aquae Sulis. In places it survives; elsewhere no apparent trace remains in view.

row.old_value: A Bronze Age henge on Eyam Moor in the Peak District with 10 upright orthostats. Its earthen bank exceeds 30 metres in diameter — the largest stone circle of its type in the county.
row.new_value: On Eyam Moor, with clear views of the River Derwent valley, Wet Withens is the largest embanked stone circle in Derbyshire. Its Chair Stone has a ledge cut out of its face, like a seat.

row.old_value: A Roman villa with an aisled hall and bath house, rebuilt multiple times over four centuries. A new bath complex was added in the 2nd-3rd century as the villa expanded.
row.new_value: The first substantial villa found south of the Purbeck Hills, Bucknowle Roman Villa began in the late 1st century AD with an aisled hall and grew to three large buildings and a bath house.

row.old_value: A 1585 sketch of Aldgate's north tower reveals an interior room of approximately 16 by 14 foot; its southern sibling probably had similar dimensions.
row.new_value: Aldgate once pierced the defensive wall around the City of London. In 1377, fearing a French attack, it was fortified with portcullises and chains; its defences were tested twice.

row.old_value: Carrigagulla is a megalithic complex 2.9 km north-east of Ballinagree, County Cork. Carrigagulla A is an 8-metre-diameter stone circle consisting of 16 standing stones circling a central slab.
row.new_value: Near Ballinagree in County Cork, Carrigagulla gathers a circle of 16 standing stones around a central slab, and a stone row where four of five stones have been moved and now serve as gates.

row.old_value: A D-shaped semi-broch sharing a valley with two full brochs, Dun Telve and Dun Troddan. Its half-circular design suggests a transitional building form between duns and brochs.
row.new_value: In the upper reaches of Gleann Beag stands Dun Grugaig, a D-shaped fort of a type commonly regarded as a prototype broch, sharing its valley with the brochs of Dun Telve and Dun Troddan.

row.old_value: Third-largest Maya site in the Three River region, La Milpa was active 400 BC-850 AD. Pyramid-centred and positioned where two major borders converge, it was a key hub in the regional trade network.
row.new_value: Amid farming terraces in northwest Belize lies La Milpa, a Maya city whose Main Plaza alone covers 18,000 square meters. In the mid-8th century, its monuments and stelae multiplied.

row.old_value: Dating to around 250 BC, Maes Knoll covers 8 hectares with a rampart rising 14 metres. The Wansdyke — a post-Roman frontier bank — meets the fort at its eastern edge.
row.new_value: At the eastern end of the Dundry Down ridge, south of Bristol, stands Maes Knoll, an Iron Age hill fort whose name joins a Brythonic word for flat top with an Old English word for hill.

row.old_value: Guitarrero Cave has evidence of human use around 8,000 BCE and possibly as early as 10,560 BCE.
row.new_value: In the Callejón de Huaylas valley, Guitarrero Cave held some of South America's earliest cultivated plants, with evidence of human use around 8,000 BCE and possibly as early as 10,560 BCE.

row.old_value: The flint mine, which was levelled about 1950, is on the south-west slope of Blackpatch Hill.
row.new_value: On the south-west slope of Blackpatch Hill lie more than 64 infilled shafts of a Neolithic flint mine, galleries once reaching up to 8.5 metres along a single seam of flint.

row.old_value: Maya site active 250–950 AD in the Petexbatún region. Three groups — north, east, and west — share a main plaza and acropolis, arranged across a defended peninsula.
row.new_value: Across the neck of its peninsula on Lake Petexbatún, the Maya site of Punta de Chimino dug three moats, one 12 metres deep, each topped by a palisaded wall, with box gardens between.

row.old_value: A Roman villa with piers stretching into the sea, fish ponds, moray eel farms, and a rich library. Consul Lucullus was famous for his legendary feasts.
row.new_value: Built in Naples in the first century BC, the Villa of Lucullus had piers stretching into the sea. Its remains are visible at several places, and Roman columns still stand in a castle cellar.

row.old_value: The dolmen sits at the southern end of a large cairn, of approximately 30x10 metres, the north end of which also contains a cist.
row.new_value: At the foot of Slieve Gullion, the granite capstone of Ballykeel Dolmen balances on the tips of three portal stones. Its chamber held three highly decorated Ballyalton bowls.

row.old_value: Bronze Age burial mounds in Somerset, its medieval name 'Battlegore' attached after a Danish raid in 918 AD. Three round barrows, possibly a long chambered barrow, referenced since the 14th century.
row.new_value: Three round barrows, and possibly a long chambered one, make up Battlegore Burial Chamber in Somerset, where bronze finds include a rapier, a spearhead, a winged axe and a broken dagger.

row.old_value: The fortress is rectangular, and was built with four gates and 22 towers along the circuit of walls enclosing the site; 18 of the towers still survive.
row.new_value: At the mouth of the Chorokhi river on the Black Sea, the Roman walls of Gonio Fortress still keep 18 of their 22 towers. Its oldest mention comes from Pliny the Elder, in the 1st century AD.

row.old_value: A circular Iron Age fort covering 2.8 hectares, linked to the Catuvellauni and Trinovantes tribes. Its rampart and steep bank survive today.
row.new_value: A rampart and steep banked slope ringed South Weald Camp in Essex, a 2.8 hectare hillfort thought to be late Iron Age, later part of a deer-park and then a WWII training ground.

row.old_value: In a series of excavations between 1984 and 1985 Palaeolithic stone artifacts and Pleistocene faunal remains were uncovered.
row.new_value: Trou de l'Abîme, a cave by the Eau Noire, yielded Palaeolithic flint brought from a mine at least 30 km away and a partial human molar no one could then call Homo sapiens or Neanderthal.

row.old_value: The Grey Mare and her Colts is a megalithic chambered long barrow located near Abbotsbury in Dorset.
row.new_value: Near Abbotsbury lies the Grey Mare and her Colts, a Neolithic chambered long barrow of 3400-2400 BC; partly excavated in the early nineteenth century, it held human bones and pottery.

row.old_value: A 3rd-century AD Roman temple perched on a hill in the Beqaa Valley. Part of a complex blending Roman imperial religion with local Phoenician traditions.
row.new_value: The Hosn Niha Roman Temple site lies at the base of a steep slope near the Beqaa Valley. Its Upper Great Temple faces east from a podium: four columns, a cella, then an elevated adytum.

row.old_value: Caves used as a necropolis from the Paleolithic through the Neolithic. Finds are split across two museums — the caves themselves are rarely open to the public.
row.new_value: In Cascais, evidence points to use of the Caves of Poço Velho as a necropolis, with around 115 burials identified. Finds include limestone votive offerings and decorated schist slabs.

row.old_value: Occupied 50 BC to 5th century AD, starting as a late Iron Age settlement before Roman construction created a large villa. Its finds are displayed in a deconsecrated 1851 chapel on the village edge.
row.new_value: Workmen digging for limestone in 1781 rediscovered Piddington Roman Villa, a winged-corridor villa whose 2nd-century well is probably the largest stone-lined well in Roman Britain.

row.old_value: A hilltop with a Bronze Age barrow, a menhir, and a logan stone that supposedly could only be rocked at midnight. The menhir stands on the western slope near an old mine.
row.new_value: A round barrow crowns the summit of Trink Hill, 212 metres high near Nancledra, with a trig point set within it, and on the western slope stands a stone named after the nearby Giew Mine.

row.old_value: Iron Age earthworks consisting of a hill, a mound, and a rectangular enclosure connected by a zigzag causeway. They date to 395-205 BC and sit inside Hatfield Forest.
row.new_value: In Hatfield Forest, a zig-zag causeway formed by 2 almost parallel ditches links the mound of Portingbury Hills to an enclosure. Digs in 1964–1965 found a small flint blade 4 cm long.

row.old_value: A Maya pyramid built around 250 BC, largely destroyed in 2013 by contractors mining it for road gravel. Only the core of the once-massive structure survived.
row.new_value: At Nohmul, a Maya pyramid about 17 meters tall rose around 250 BC. Largely abandoned, it seems, by the 5th century, the site was later reoccupied and holds about 700 visible mounds.

row.old_value: Minoan cave 400 m above sea level on Mt. Juktas, Crete. Used from Neolithic times as refuge and burial, then inhabited in Early Minoan times.
row.new_value: On the southwest slope of Mount Juktas, Stravomyti Cave first saw use in Neolithic times as a refuge and burial, and may once have been a shrine to Artemis, Diktynna or perhaps Eileithyia.

row.old_value: Occupied around 35,000 BC, this cave near Châtelperron sits at the boundary between Neanderthal and modern human toolmaking traditions. Its artifacts define the Châtelperronian culture.
row.new_value: La Grotte des Fées: two interlinked caves discovered around 1840, perhaps in 1848, during railway construction. Several thousand flint blades and mammoth tusks over 2 metres long were found.

row.old_value: Peyre-Brune is a Neolithic dolmen situated near Saint-Aquilin in the department of the Dordogne.
row.new_value: Surrounded by woods on a rise near Saint-Aquilin in the Dordogne, Peyre-Brune is a Neolithic dolmen: one rectangular chamber, the burial tomb of a local chieftain who was not incinerated.

row.old_value: The first Bronze Age site found in the country, with burials containing pottery filled with animal bones, beads, and spear points. No iron was found, helping date the site precisely.
row.new_value: In the Bronze Age cemetery of Nyaung-gan, 43 individuals were found, most buried with the head pointing north. It was the first site in Myanmar to have artefacts dating to the Bronze Age.

row.old_value: 3300-500 BC Bronze Age settlement clusters on Bodmin Moor at 329 metres. Two settlement areas on the slopes hold field enclosures, cairns, a cist, a propped stone, and associated stone circles.
row.new_value: Leskernick Hill stands 329m high on Bodmin Moor. On its south and western slopes lie 2 Bronze Age settlements, with field enclosures, small cairns, a cist and a propped stone.

row.old_value: Maya site dated to 400 BC with three stelae and an altar arranged as an E-Group astronomical complex. A monument to Maya celestial observation, active from the Late Preclassic period.
row.new_value: On an east-facing scarp, the three stelae and altar of Tres Islas mimic the E-Group at Uaxactun, a perfect place to watch the sunrise at this Early Classic Maya capital.

row.old_value: The archaeological complex of Caballo Muerto features stone and adobe constructions, with mud used as mortar.
row.new_value: In the Moche Valley, Caballo Muerto holds a dozen ceremonial buildings on platforms, walls decorated with reliefs of snakes and cats, its people living off land reclaimed from the desert.

row.old_value: An Iron Age cliff castle near Land's End, one of only two fortified sites in its county where early Iron Age pottery has been found. A stone rampart blocks the only landward approach.
row.new_value: Near Land's End, a stone rampart and ditch cut across a headland with almost sheer cliffs on two sides: Maen Castle, one of only two Cornish fortified sites to yield Early Iron Age pottery.

row.old_value: A multivallate Durotrigian hillfort crowns a 277-metre hill in Dorset. Fourteen hut foundations found within suggest a sizable settled community on the summit.
row.new_value: The 277-metre hill of Pilsdon Pen, at the north end of the Marshwood Vale, is crowned by an Iron Age Durotrigian hillfort. Near its centre, the remains of 14 roundhouses were uncovered.

row.old_value: At 10.5 hectares, Ladle Hill's fort was never finished. Unexcavated but sharply defined, its interrupted ditches reveal the step-by-step construction method Iron Age builders used.
row.new_value: Ladle Hill is perhaps the best known of Britain's unfinished hillforts: dumps of material from the abandoned works lie inside, and it has long been suspected no settlement stood there.

row.old_value: Ruins of a Punic-Roman sanctuary on Gozo's southwest coast, dating from 1500 BC to the 4th century AD. The promontory site was used for millennia.
row.new_value: On the southwest coast of Gozo, the promontory of Ras il-Wardija holds a Punic-Roman sanctuary. Carved crosses on its walls suggest it later became a Christian place of worship.

row.old_value: The westernmost gate of London's Roman wall, rebuilt several times before its demolition in 1760. Its name survives in Ludgate Hill, the street leading to St. Paul's Cathedral.
row.new_value: Ludgate was the westernmost gate in London Wall, believed to be one of its four original Roman gates. A legend recorded by Geoffrey of Monmouth names it after the ancient British King Lud.

row.old_value: A small round earthwork that looks defensive but was actually an Iron Age farmstead. Dense woodland now obscures its modest banks and ditches.
row.new_value: Thick woods in Somerset cloak Wraxall Camp, an Iron Age settlement whose homes sat within a bank and ditch. Digs in 1928 found black burnished pottery and a Kimmeridge shale bracelet.

row.old_value: A Roman road named after a 15th-century doctor — "gate" comes from the Scandinavian word for road. It connected two forts across the Peak District.
row.new_value: Between the forts of Glossop and Brough-on-Noe ran Doctor's Gate, a Roman road named for Dr John Talbot, credited with improving its summit in the late 15th century.

row.old_value: A Roman earthwork with two parallel banks 20 m apart and a channel between them. Its original length was over 550 metres; pottery sherds from the early Roman period date the construction.
row.new_value: Raw Dykes in Leicester: two parallel Roman banks with a channel between, once at least 550 metres long, now 110 metres. In the English Civil War, Royalists set artillery on part of it.

row.old_value: An altar set up in the Athenian Agora in 522 BC as the city's central milestone. All distances from Athens were measured from this single point.
row.new_value: In the Classical Agora of Athens stood the Altar of the Twelve Gods, a place of supplication and refuge and, from at least the 5th century BC, the zero point for distances to Athens.

row.old_value: A Neolithic ritual center from 5300 BC with scattered remains of over 1,000 people from distant communities. The bones show signs of systematic defleshing.
row.new_value: In 1996 a building site gave up bones and human skulls: Herxheim, a Neolithic ritual center and mass grave, estimated to hold the scattered remains of more than 1000 individuals.

row.old_value: A Roman temple to Proserpina, goddess of the underworld. Its marble was later stripped and reused across Valletta—only one piece survives in place.
row.new_value: Marble ruins found in 1613 at Mtarfa: the Temple of Proserpina, goddess of the underworld. Its inscription says it was already old and near collapse when Chrestion restored it.

row.old_value: Roman Iron Age cemetery east of Herning, dated 200–400 AD. Grave 83 yielded only a preserved complex hairstyle — the elaborate coiffure of a young woman archaeologists named the Hammerum Girl.
row.new_value: Of the Hammerum Girl, buried in the late Roman Iron Age, only a complex coiffure survives, beside unusually well-preserved clothing, in a grave of the Hammerum Burial Site near Herning.

row.old_value: Much of the road exists as an exceptionally large embankment, up to 50 ft wide and 6 ft high.
row.new_value: Up to 50 ft wide and 6 ft high, the embankment of Ackling Dyke carries a Roman road straight through prehistoric barrows, a sight that must have been meant to impress the native population.

row.old_value: El Salt is an archaeological site from the Middle Paleolithic near Alcoy which was frequented by groups of archaic humans for thousands of years.
row.new_value: Beneath a limestone wall 38 meters high, Neanderthals at El Salt left fire pits, flint tools and six teeth at least 50,000 years ago, and coprolites showing their diets included plants.

row.old_value: Circular dwellings alongside rectangular chullpa burial towers at high altitude. Chullpas housed the dead above ground, as if they never truly left.
row.new_value: On the slopes of Pitaq Mach'ay in the Huánuco Region, Tikra holds circular buildings and square or rectangular burial towers, a site declared National Cultural Heritage in 2001.

row.old_value: Caves and stone buildings on a forested Rhone valley hill, inhabited continuously from the Neolithic until the early 20th century. A chapel from 1706, partly built in a cave, still stands.
row.new_value: Above the Rhône valley, the caves and stone buildings of the Barry Troglodyte Village were inhabited from the neolithic to the early 20th century, their chapel of 1706 partly set in a cave.

row.old_value: Three granite uprights carry a 4.5 by 3.1 m capstone on Shilstone Farm near Drewsteignton. The structure collapsed in 1862 and was rebuilt the same year.
row.new_value: On Shilstone Farm near Drewsteignton, three granite supports of Spinsters' Rock hold up a capstone of 4.5 by 3.1 metres. The Neolithic dolmen collapsed in 1862 and was restored that year.
On a western slope of Uma Urqu north of Ayacucho, Wichqana was a ceremonial center from around 1200-800 BC, with semicircle temple structures raised on artificial mounds.

row.old_value: An Iron Age fort classified as a "slight univallate hillfort." Two sections of banks survive in what is now a nature reserve managed by a wildlife trust.
row.new_value: Thought to be the fort the Viking Hastein built in 894, the Danish Camp in Essex has yielded no trace of Viking occupation, but Middle Iron Age pottery and four round houses instead.

row.old_value: A dolmen group with nine large stones forming a polygonal burial chamber and a two-part corridor. A communal funerary site from the 3rd millennium BC.
row.new_value: La Chabola de la Hechicera, a dolmen in Elvillar, held human remains and a polished axe of ophite. Its top stone, found broken into three parts, was restored to its assumed place in 1974.

row.old_value: Two moose carved onto a rock near the river Fossen — one 31 cm, the other 35 cm. Dating to the 6th millennium BC, their position beside the river leaves them submerged during high water levels.
row.new_value: Near the river Fossen, the Rock Carvings at Eidefoss show two moose, measuring 31 centimetres and 35 centimetres, on a rock that may have fallen from a nearly vertical cliff.

row.old_value: An Iron Age village continuously occupied for 500 years, with entrance graves, field systems, and standing stones also on site. A rare intact prehistoric landscape.
row.new_value: On St Mary's in the Isles of Scilly, Halangy Down keeps an Iron Age village of attached stone houses on four terraces; digs found bronze brooches, millstones and a slate spindle-whorl.

row.old_value: A circle of 55 close-set slate stones, 26.8 m across, with a southeast entrance gap. The Lake District saw more stone circles built than almost anywhere.
row.new_value: Beside Swinside Fell in southern Cumbria, the stone circle of Swinside, also called Sunkenkirk, opens to the south-east between two large portal stones set outside its ring of slate.

row.old_value: Four tall standing stones arranged in ascending height across 13.4 metres -- the largest stone row of over 80 in the southwest. The tallest stone stands 3.4 metres.
row.new_value: Castlenalacht Stone Row, the largest of over 80 stone rows in south-west Ireland, sets four tall stones in rising height across 13.4 m on a Cork hilltop. Their precise function is unknown.

row.old_value: Herefordshire Beacon's shape is entirely determined by the terraced Iron Age earthworks, compared to a giant wedding cake. A Norman castle was added later atop this 2nd-century BC fortification.
row.new_value: Atop Herefordshire Beacon in the Malvern Hills, British Camp's earthworks have been compared to a giant wedding cake: an Iron Age hill fort thought first built in the 2nd century BC.

row.old_value: At Takht-e Soleyman, this Atash Behram — Zoroastrianism's highest fire grade — served the warrior class. The only one of three supreme fires whose temple has been physically located.
row.new_value: Sasanian kings built the Azargoshnasp Fire Temple for one of the three most sacred fires of pre-Islamic Iran. Heraclius sacked it in 623/4, yet the fire burned on into the Islamic era.

row.old_value: The remains of the Mithraeum in Konjic were discovered in January 1897, at the banks of river Trešanica, under village Repovci, on the outskirts of Konjic.
row.new_value: By the river Trešanica stood the Konjic Mithraeum, an early 4th century AD temple to Mithra. Its gray limestone relief shows a Tauroctony on one side and a ritual meal on the other.

row.old_value: A 6th-9th century AD Maya city with over 200 structures, only a few excavated. It was an independent city before becoming a tributary of nearby Copán.
row.new_value: In the Florida Valley, Arqueológico El Puente Park holds more than 200 Maya structures, from tombs to living quarters. Only a few have been excavated, among them a large step pyramid.

row.old_value: A multivallate hillfort near Steeple Langford, Wiltshire, occupied from around 300 BC. A 1991 survey found 130 internal structures alongside Iron Age and Roman coins, pottery, and human burials.
row.new_value: Three ramparts with outer ditches ring Yarnbury Castle, an Iron Age hillfort in Wiltshire. Around 130 structures hint at long settlement, and an earlier, smaller enclosure lies at its heart.

row.old_value: Early Classic Maya site active 250–600 AD in the Petén jungle. Covers 1.3 square kilometres with 729 major structures, near the borders of two neighbouring countries in dense tropical forest.
row.new_value: Río Azul, a Maya site of funerary pyramids and ornate tombs, some of them corbel-vaulted, holds an inscription dated to AD 393 that names the Teotihuacan warlord Siyaj K'ak'.

row.old_value: A cave in a limestone massif with a 372 m route and an entrance at 885 m elevation. It preserves evidence of prehistoric use deep within.
row.new_value: Simanya Cave has a 372 m route in the Sant Llorenç del Munt massif. Chalcolithic ceramics were found in 1911; between 1929 and 1930, Pau Codina's surveys found a large amount of pottery.
